speechtext: No, they do not include dependents. The total number of people who receive benefits from the pensions, is very large. There are 146,373 people in Canada coming under the benefit of pensions. That includes disability pensioners, and their dependents, and dependent pensioners and their dependents.

I take it that there will be a good deal of discussion of the question of pensions, and I think it will be rather difficult to keep separate the matters that refer to pensions and to Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment work. In other words there are cases which, if they were admitted to treatment under the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment for disabilities at the front, would, generally speaking, be eligible for pensions. Therefore, there may be some difficulty in separating them. I know that the few remarks I am going to make a little later on will probably combine them. Has the minister any objection to a certain amount of intermingling of these estimates? I suppose what is said in this discussion will not be repeated on the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment estimates. It is very difficult to keep them separate. I make this statement in order to allow the chairman to take a lenient view of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: At the time I had the honour to submit to the House the estimate in connection with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment I gave a statement of the number of soldiers under treatment. When a soldier is in the hospital his pension is paid to him just the same, and the amount is made up to the amount he would receive if he received full pay and allowance. The amounts I have mentioned refer only to pensions which are awarded by the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada. This amount has no reference whatever to the treatment of patients, or the maintenance of hospitals, or the examination of pensioners, or the examination of soldiers who desire to receive treatment, it simply covers the amount of money awarded to pensioners in Canada, and nothing else.

I wish to say a few words in connection with the pensions matter, as the people of my constituency are particularly interested in this work. The Pensions Act has been administered now for a number of years, and we have had an opportunity of discovering a good many flaws in the administration. I do not know that anyone in particular is to blame, but the spirit of the act, I think, has not been carried out in the way that was intended when it was passed. It has been unsatisfactory, not only to those that are directly affected by the working of the act, but also to the public who from one end of Canada to the other, are highly desirous to render the fullest possible service and full justice particularly to those men who went overseas and so nobly fought the battle for this country. We can never hope to compensate them fully for what they have done for us. But we should make every effort possible, to the extent even of our last dollar, to do justice to those men, and not only to see that they are paid proper pensions for their disabilities, but, in addition to that, to aim to restore to them their usefulness, and in that way add to their peace of mind. It is complained by these men that the Pension Act is inconsistent in some ways. In some cases it is said the pensions are entirely inadequate when the disability is taken into consideration. Then again it is complained that in the case of, say, two men affected almost in the same way and to the same extent with regard to their ability to earn a living, one man is paid a much higher pension than the other. It has been claimed also that a man who has had severe head injuries, suffering from extreme nervousness, unable to concentrate his mind on his work, suffering from headaches and dizziness, and unable on that account to hold any position.
Supply-S.C.R.-Pensions

is given a pension of $5 per month. It is said that one of the principal sufferers is the man who carried on overseas, the man who, though affected with sickness, probably suffering to a certain extent from gas or other causes, still persisted in carrying on his work, with the result that when he arrived on this side, and began to really suffer from the effects of the war, he was unable to show any history of having been under treatment on the other side. Anyone looking at the question from an ordinary business standpoint and under ordinary business conditions, would accept that as evidence that this man suffered from a disability. But his case is turned down because he is unable to show documentary proof of what occurred. Many men, it is claimed, are suffering from an injustice in this country as a result. I will read just one or two cases referred to by certain men in Victoria who have made a careful study of the situation.
This is the case of a man who enlisted on August 10, 1914, and was a prisoner of war in Germany from April 24, 1915, to March, 1918, when he was sent to Holland. He arrived in England December 19, 1918. He had, of course, no medical history sheet. On his arrival in England his only anxiety was to get back to Canada, and for that purpose he declared himself fit. As a matter of fact, the man was greatly run down and had suffered in Germany from severe pains in the abdomen lasting several weeks at a time. He was discharged from the army on May 3, 1919, at Victoria. He suffered continually from gastric trouble. In February, 1922, he went to the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; he was given treatment, but was refused pay and allowances. On applying for pension for which, of course, it should not have been necessary for him to apply, as he should have been examined for pension, he was told that he could not receive a pension because he could not supply medical evidence of his illness in Germany. Subsequently he filed a declaration by a Lieutenant McDowall, who was his officer and who was a prisoner with him in Germany, whose evidence substantiated his statement as to the nature of his illness while a prisoner. This evidence was refused, and he is not yet in receipt of a pension. He is now a physical wreck.
Here is another case of a private who enlisted in Victoria, June 1, 1916. He went to France December 1, 1916, and served twenty-seven months in the trenches. All the time he was not in good health, but he carried on. He was discharged December 19, 1919, as Al. He took up land under the Soldier Settlement

Board, but he broke down before going on to the land. He is married and as he says, he thanks God he has no children. He is in very straitened circumstances, and is in very poor health. He has applied to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment from time to time, but he has been refused any amelioration. On December 20, 1919, two months after his discharge, he was admitted to the Jubilee hospital, suffering from gastric ulcers and toxic poisoning, and was extremely ill. The doctor placed him on treatment with pay and allowances. Ottawa refused pay and allowances and subsequently even treatment. On February 10, 1922, after an interval of continuous suffering and treatment by private doctors, who all say that his condition is due to war service, he again applied to the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and the local doctor placed him again in hospital. During this hospital period the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment doctor had all his teeth removed save six, Dr. Arnold, Medical Director of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, directed that he should receive no pay and allowances, and pension also was refused by him. The treatment then continued. On October 18. 1922, the sub-unit office in Victoria asked the Vancouver office for a denture to supply the place of removed teeth. On October 28, 1922, Dr. Proctor, of Vancouver, Medical Director of the "J" Unit, refused to give any denture and ordered that all treatment must cease. The man was then placed in the charity ward, and he subsequently received treatment from the local doctors, out of charity. Here we have the fact of a gallant soldier who wished to cany on and not make a fuss, having his very gallantry used to his detriment by the Pension board, because he reported Al to get back to Canada. No Pension board ever examined this man. The case was entirely decided by doctors. The man is still suffering severely, but he is doing his best. Naturally enough he cannot compete in the labour market.
The third and last case I have is that of a widow whose first husband was a member of the 16th Battalion. He was killed in action and a pension was granted to his wife and one child. On December 19, 1916, this lady remarried a pay sergeant in the 50th Highlanders who, owing to bad sight, was not allowed to go to either England or France. By him she had one child. Whilst at Willows camp, Victoria, this sergeant contracted pneumonia, and subsequently contracted influenza, and he had to leave the service. Later on he contracted tuberculosis and died of tuberculosis in February, 1922. According to doctors' statements in Victoria, this showed a clear

Supply-S.C.R.-Pensions
case of continuity from the tuberculosis to the pneumonia contracted on service. Nevertheless she was refused a pension because she cannot produce evidence that her husband contracted tuberculosis whilst on service, or any evidence of the nature or possible cause of the disability which led to his death. This information should have been on the man's military papers and medical history sheet; but no such documents in his case can be found, and the evidence goes to show that they were probably burnt up in the fire which took place at the Work Point barracks. The widow is at present living on charity, with her two children. She still draws a small pension for the first child.
These are cases, not only of lives lost, but of lives ruined as the result of the war. If it was not the intention of the Pension Act to meet just such cases as I have cited, what did we pass that act through the House for? In my opinion, it was passed for the purpose of relieving just such cases as these, and in the administration of the act more elasticity will have to be given or great injustice will be done to men who deserve much better treatment. These complaints are coming in, not by ones or twos, but by hundreds, and I am informed that if the resolution proposed by the minister takes the form of legislation later on, no fewer than 10,000 cases on appeal will be presented for his decision. It is quite clear then that the 'act< under present 'conditions Ss not fulfilling its mission. The people have waited and asked for reform; they have been very patient; they have given a great deal of time for the carrying out of the administration of this act so as to enable little discrepancies to be overcome. But results have not been reassuring as might be expected, and consequently we find that the people in some sections now are getting very much excited over the condition of affairs. On June 29 last, a very representative mass meeting was held in Victoria, British Columbia. At that meeting the following bodies were represented: Liberal Association, Independent Order of Foresters, Trades and Labour Council, the Council of the municipality of Oak Bay, the Council of the municipality of Esquimalt, the Kumtuks Club, Gyro Club, Rotary Club, Kiwanis Club, Army and Navy Veterans, Women's Conservative Association, Grand Army of United Veterans, Salvation Army, Navy League, Chamber of Commerce, Conservative Association, Women's Canadian Club, Canadian Club, Young Mens Christian Association, Saanich Council, Tubercular Veterans Association and British
Campaigners. Among those present were the Bishop of Columbia, and Father Wood representing St. Andrews Cathedral. This meeting was also a very representative one of the principal citizens of Victoria, and at it the following resolution was passed by a unanimous standing vote:
Whereas the findings of the Royal Commission on Pensions constitute a grave indictment of the Pension board in their administration of the Pension board and shows that the members thereof are unfitted to fairly administer the act:
Resolved, that in the opinion of this meeting of representative public men and women of Victoria, the government forthwith take the necessary steps to remove the members of the Pension board from office:
And further, be it resolved that copies of this resolution be sent to the Premier, members of the Cabinet and members for British Columbia in the Senate and House of Commons.
This was a non-political gathering, and I am very well acquainted with a large number of those who were present on that occasion. The gentleman who acted as chairman is the editor of the Liberal newspaper in Victoria. The resolution was moved by the Lord Bishop of British Columbia and seconded by the secretary of the Trades and Labour Council. Since that time I have received a wire from the Canadian Club, the Chamber of Commerce, the Rotary, the Kiwanis and the Gyro Clubs, besides soldier organizations, which have all either endorsed the resolution or forwarded similar resolutions asking for reform This will indicate that the feeling is general throughout that section of Canada, and it clearly shows that there is a very urgent demand for immediate reform. The principal speaker of the evening on the occasion in question was Major Twigg, a soldier who had been overseas and a lawyer of considerable ability. He claimed that seventy-five per cent of the returned soldier cases in which applications were made for pensions never reached the board at all but were settled by doctors, and that in many cases, where fifty per cent disability had been recommended by doctors, only twenty per cent was allowed by the board. He declared that there was apparent an effort to practise economy at the expense of the men. I quote the following from a newspaper report of the meeting:
Mr. Twigg took up various phases of the pensions question. A woman whose husband died from cancer five minutes before the official end of the war, said he. would be given a pension by the Board; while one whose husband died five minutes after the hour set down would not. The pension board took the stand that the statute was there and had to be enforced, and asked whether he thought that the board was following out the intention of parliament in regard to the above-mentioned situation, the head of the board had said, "I think so."

Another quotation from the address of Major Twigg is as follows:
Mr. Twigg cited the case of a man gassed at Ypres. He had been a big husky chap before the war. Gassed, he had reported to the doctor that he could not stop coughing. The doctor said, "Everybody's coughing; carry on," and the man had carried on, no record being made on his medical history sheet. Bronchial pneumonia developed, and the man spent a long period in hospitals. Finally he asked for a pension. He was refused treatment, refused pay and allowances, and refused pensions because no mention of his being gassed had been made on the medical history sheet. The man was now dying because of the decision of the pension board, and the worry accompanying his efforts to care for his family. The men who carried on without running to the doctor every time anything was the matter with them were the ones who suffered in the matter of pensions. The men who always went to the doctor had medical history sheet evidence. Pension after pension had been refused because men had no evidence on their medical history sheet to prove that their disabilities had come from service.
Major Twigs also claimed that although the 1920 amendments were held by the board to refer to the permanent force, in reality they were manipulated to cover men who had been overseas. It was claimed that this was at the bottom of the agitation throughout Canada. Speaking of the proposed resolution Major Twigg reminded the audience that it was not so much that the law was at fault as that the administration was to blame. This criticism of the Pension board was dispassionately presented. And, as I have stated, I am acquainted with a great many of those who were at the meeting and know them to be leading citizens and not firebrands. Their one aim was to do justice to the returned soldiers. We must remember that the returned soldier did not stop to bargain with us when called upon to go overseas but gallantly joined the forces. He set aside all business or other arrangements, his hopes were all sidetracked, and he subordinated his ambition and his desires to the impulse to render service to his country. We feel therefore that these men, having left their dependents at home under these circumstances, should receive justice now at the hands of the country. In my opinion they are entitled to the very last dollar which it is reasonably within our ability to pay them. When a gathering of the kind I have described passes a drastic resolution such as I have read, it indicates how acute the conditions are and how necessary it is that immediate action should be taken.
I can quite understand the difficulties of a board of this character, who have a vast variety of cases presented to them and who naturally desire to keep within the law. But if they hftve not the power now, then they certainly should be given that power, to apply a

certain degree of elasticity to their administration of the act. In my opinion what is required is good judgment tempered with sympathy and mercy in all cases.
It is quite apparent from what I have quoted that the Pension Act is not achieving just exactly what we had expected, and the matter is too serious to be allowed to drift any longer. I am very glad indeed to note that the minister has presented to the House certain resolutions which promise to afford relief in the directions complained of; and so far as I can see, before the question has been debated, I think they should tend to make the situation very much better than it is now.
As regards1 the administration of the act, clearly it was the desire of the House representing the people of Canada, when that act was passed, to take care of just such cases as I have mentioned, and hundreds of others that have been sidetracked simply because they could not comply with some little technicality in the law. It would be far better to give the act a much broader interpretation, even at the expense possibly of overpaying some fellows who might be inclined to fake, than
4 p.m. by too great stringency to rob hundreds of men and their dependents of the pensions that are justly due them under the law as it stands now. We cannot be too merciful or too sympathetic or considerate in cases of this kind. As I have said before, these young men when they joined the colours to go overseas parted with their family connections and renounced the prospects that they had seen ahead of them. No doubt many of them had had a vision of that point of efficiency, after certain years of hard work, at which they would be able to establish themselves, to marry and settle down in homes of their own. Many of them have come back badly maimed, some physically, others mentally, with the result that they find themselves unable to make a living and with all their hopes for a, bright and happy future entirely gone by the board. These cases should receive the most careful attention, and I am sure it is the wish of the Canadian people from one end of the country to the other to render them justice in the fullest possible measure.

Mr. Chairman, if there is an instance where the distribution of the public funds should be carried out with the utmost fairness, it is certainly when the question arises of granting to those disabled in the Great War a pecuniary help in compensation for the sacrifices they made for civilization. Ever since my

Difficulties in interpretation have arisen election to this House, numerous claims have been submitted to me by the dependents of the heroes who gave up their lives on the battlefields, and by those who have come to end their days in this country, burdened with infirmities due to wounds received in the war. Many have given me to understand that their cases had not been taken up by the Commission in charge of the distribution of these public funds. I have here the claim of a mother of a family from the County of Gloucester, whose son, her only support, lost his life on the battlefields. After making inquiries, the Secretary of the Commission on Pensions, informed me that the case of Mrs. Albert-that is her name-had not reached the Commission. In the second para-praph of this letter, which is signed by Mr. Davis, we come across the following lines:
No ap.plication for pension was filed on behalf of Mrs. Albert prior to your 'letter of the 10th of March last. Immediately that was received the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment yvas requested to obtain a properly completed application to investigate and report upon the case. This request is dated March 14th.
You may judge, Mr. Chairman, by this communication received from the Secretary of the Commission, that the full responsibility and care devolve upon the soldiers' dependents to acquaint the Commission of their rights.
It seems to me that in the remote parts of the country, as for instance in the back parishes of my county, these dependents should receive the necessary information so as to facilitate the task of placing their claims before the Commission.
In another instance, a farmer of my county, a Mr. Comeau, belonging to the parish of Petit Rocher is liable to lose his farm, which is already heavily mortgaged. An official came to him and made him sign a declaration that the crop on his farm was sufficient for the support of his family and that moreover he had, each year, a net balance of $300. When I made inquiries in regard to the matter, I was able to ascertain that instead of a net balance of $300 per year, this farmer had only sold $300 worth of products during the year. He had to meet from the above income rather heavy taxes as well as the interest on his mortgage. He is advancing in age, his health is on the decline and he will soon become a public charge unless help is extended to him. Now, how does it happen that these farmers, these heads of families having given what is most precious to them, their sons, in defence of this country, should be required to sign documents void of truth? I have made inquiries on the subject, and if I am well
informed, it appears that these good people are at the mercy of these investigators and are not in a position to understand the purport of the statement which is required of them. That is why I have requested from the hon. minister, and I again make this request from my seat, that a French-speaking official, be sent into my county so as to make an inquiry into each case and thus do what is right towards those whose sacrifice was great in the war.
The correspondence received on the subject is very voluminous. I might read it out and give the Committee an idea of the different claims that I have received, however, I hope this will not be necessary, and that with the hon. minister's help and the commissioners' good will, the demands of ex-service men, having taken part in the Great War or their dependents will be taken under consideration and that justice will be dealt out to them. I strongly insist that each interested person should receive the necessary forms and instructions so as to enable him to put in his claims. It seems to me unfair to insert in the statutes of our country laws governing the disabled in the Great War and to force upon these good people the burden of putting into practice the different regulations enacted in their favour by the Dominion government. If for example, circular letters were addressed to each of these soldiers or their dependents, explaining or giving a synopsis of the act, it would help in making the administration of the act easier. I trust that this suggestion will be taken into serious consideration and that the disabled in the Great War not only from my county but from all the counties of Canada will be thoroughly informed on this matter and that in future we may witness a little more fairness in the distribution of the public funds.

While we are on the subject of pensions I would like to take this opportunity of referring to the difficulties which a number of applicants for pensions have in getting their cases fully investigated and their claims adequately met. I have been recently informed that through the efforts of the Great War Veterans' Association about six hundred cases have received substantial pension adjustment in the past twelve months. If that be the case, and I have been assured that it is, it shows that there is a difficulty in applicants securing a full investigation of their claims at the outset, and that it has required a further effort and assistance through an organization to have their claims fully and forcibly presented so that they have now obtained a better treatment than they were accorded at the outset. This number does not include minor adjustments that have been obtained, but as I said before, there are six hundred applicants who after their cases had been taken up through the organization of the Great War Veterans' Association have

received substantial pension adjustments. That is a point which I bring forward as one of those important in the future, so that we may enable those who claim pensions to obtain what is their due with a reasonable amount of facility. I have no doubt there are many claims presented of an exaggerated character, but clearly these are not of that character because they have been granted finally.
There is one particular case that I wish to bring to the attention of the committee which bears on the same subject. It is that of a nursing sister who in her early childhood had a severe injury to her hip, from which she duly recovered. She was passed as fit in Canada and again passed as fit in England, and proceeded to France. She was in the Expeditionary Force from the 12th April, 1915, to the 1st July, 1919. During this time she served in France for three years and nine months, an unusually long period for service in France, and rendered excellent service. While in France her hip became troublesome, but not sufficiently to interfere with her duties, and she carried on. On her return to Canada she served as a nurse in one of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment hospitals, but after a time her hip became still more troublesome and she was obliged to leave the service. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment decided that it was not advisable for her to continue further her duties, suffering as she was from the condition of her hip, having the view that it would increase further her disability. She received a vocational training in typewriting. She received also four per cent disability, for an aggravation of disability, which amounted to S100. You will observe that she was discharged from the hospital as unfit for duty. Her application for pension was declined. On one letter sent to the Pension board asking for pension was a marginal note from one of the medical advisers stating:
This lady was in charge of the surgical ward of which I was the medical officer in charge in the fall of 1915, and to my personal knowledge had an obvious disability. (Difficulty in walking.)
You will observe that the term "obvious disability" occurs in the act. It is one of those conditions which preclude one from obtaining a pension; that is, if anyone goes to France suffering from an obvious disability, that is the bar against receiving a pension. Now this statement is made on the margin of her letter, and I cannot help thinking that that is a bar against receiving a pension.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to add a few remarks to those just made by my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud). the French language. With reference to pensions, many cases were referred to in this House. Among those I have here, there is one which I especially wish to submit to you. At this late date in the session, and at this stage of the proceedings, I do not wish to take up very much of the time of the House. Nevertheless, there are a few remarks that I wish to make in regard to pensions which I think are appropriate upon this occasion. It is a very difficult position to be in to discuss the workings of the Board of Pension Commissioners, for the reason that one who looks at the affairs of the country-at the tens of thousands of people who are receiving pensions, and at the millions of dollars which are annually being spent upon pensions-must feel that the task of the pension commissioners is a very difficult one. I do not wish in any way, under those circumstances, to be in the least unfair to the Pension board. I wish to preface my remarks by recognizing that they have a very difficult position, that they often have brought before them unfair and unreasonable demands and requests which are difficult to give effect to and which if given effect to on many occasions the commissioners would feel that they were not doing justice by the country. At the same time, I have had many dealings with the Board of Pension Commisioners in the past year, and in other years, and-speaking entirely for myself and not on behalf of any organization- at times it has appeared to me that the commisisoners have shown a little too great a desire for efficiency, and, perhaps, too little sympathy toward the cases coming before them. Bv sympathy I do not mean a foolish sentimentality, but that spirit of sympathy which is really meant to be inherent in the Pension Act. In other words, it has appeared to me sometimes that there is too much of an inclination on the part of the board and its officers to live up to the letter,

rather than the spirit of the law. In saying that I wish to point out that there is no personal gain for the commissioners in refusing a pension to any man. No doubt, as is mentioned in the report of the royal commission, the pension commissioners could make themselves very popular to-day among the returned soldiers by granting pensions without proper consideration. At the same time they have appeared to me at times to be a little too strict; and I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is better for them to eri on the side of leniency than that injustices should at any time be dons to the returned men. I submit, Sir, it is better, to my mind, that ten people should get pensions that do not deserve them, or that ten people should get treatment in the hospitals who do not deserve that treatment, than that one just case should be refused. I submit, in support of my statement as to a lack of sympathy-I do not say an entire lack of sympathy by any means, but at times there has been a certain lack of sympathy-the report of the royal commission. Again and again in this report the commissioners point out very much the very same conclusion as I myself arrived at before I ever read the report. For example at page 128-I do not wish to quote the statement itself because I do not desire to extend my remarks- they point out that very fact-that at times the Pension board has been " unsympathetic in its attitude." That is a synopsis of what they say; at different places in the report they point that out. I believe what the people of this country want is fairness towards the men, and after fairness has been carried out in every possible way then they want economy, but not till then. My hon friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Mac-Laren) pointed out the fact that the changed decisions proved very often that the case had not been properly considered by the board. I had a case recently where the decision was changed. The applicant in that case was a British Columbia man and his brother was a friend of mine. For that reason I took up the case but left it entirely with the Board of Pension Commissioners. I gave the board nothing but the man's own statement and the statements of medical men who had seen him. The board turned the applicant down repeatedly, but frankly his representations were so persistent, that at last I got to the stage where I threw his letters in the wastepaper basket. I heard about the case the other day. I received notice from the Board of Pension Commissioners, after I had excused them to 
him to the best of my ability, that they had granted him a pension. Well, there is something wrong, it seems to me, in a case like that, when they took so long to come to a decision. I do not know what it is, but it would appear to me that there was an error made in that case, which put me in a wrong light with the man, because I did not argue the case from any personal knowledge which I occasionally do, on account of having had a medical training and meeting a good many returned men. In that case I did not use these arguments at all, because I did not know the case. But it must have been about two years after I took up the case that the decision was changed and he got a pension. That illustrates to me that there was something wrong in handling the case in the first place. Whose fault it was I do not know. I think that case should have been given a little more consideration earlier, and that it should not have been delayed for a period of pretty nearly two years.
I might refer to another feature in this report on pensions-and I am not fond of recriminating-that practically all the severe tightening of the reins which has taken place has occurred within the last year, and I say that because I well remember that during the last election the Prime Minister, particularly-and I regret that he is not in his seat when I say this-travelled around the country pointing out that if he came to power the returned men would receive better treatment than they had been receiving. As a matter of fact, according to this report, whatever tightening up of the reins has taken place has practically taken place within the last year. I have read of very many cases quoted by the Ralston report in which that statement is borne out, but I do not wish to take up time now in reading them.
I will illustrate my other remarks by reference to another ease, though in a sense it deals more with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment than the Department of Pensions. I took the case up about a year ago with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. The name of the man was Charles McAvella. He had lived in my rdiing, but not in my city. He Came to me, and after looking over the man and listening to his history, I ascertained that he had a severe disease of the bone of the leg, what is called in medical parlance osteomyelitis He had been injured while in uniform, serving in Port Arthur. He was in the hospital a couple of weeks, got better, went overseas, served a couple of years, and was discharged

The reason I mention this matter is because the minister made a statement based on the information given him by his officials which statement was wrong. The statement was to this effect: I find that all medical reports agree that his present disability could not reasonably be attributed to his service.
I do not blame the minister. He was simply reporting what his officers told him. That statement was made to the minister, despite the fact that I put on record the opinion of a very good medical man-to say nothing of my own opinion, although I do not know that I offered my opinion medically; I know that I sent in the report of Dr. M. B.
Dean, as a medical opinion. In spite of that the officers of the department advised the minister, as he informed me, that no medical opinion agreeing that his present disability could reasonably be attributed to his service had been received. That was an absolute misstatement of fact. I then wrote to two doctors in Toronto, and I have on file the opinion of one of them. I gave him the facts of this case and when I mention his name I think all hon. members in this House will know of him, because he is probably the most outstanding surgeon in Canada. I refer to Herbert A. Bruce of Toronto. I told him the facts of the case, and I have his letter, a copy of which I shall send to the minister. He said:
Although the case you refer to evidently had no suppuration at the time of the original injury, I think one would be justified in considering that there is a very reasonable probability of the present osteomyelitis being due to the former injury.
I would consider Dr. Bruce's opinion a better opinion than that of any man in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; I would consider it a better opinion than that of any doctor or adviser on the pension board-certainly as good anyway. I think I am safe in saying that. He was for many years professor of surgery in the University of Toronto, and he has not only a national but an international reputation. The minister might ask me why I did not send the letter to him. The reason I did not send it is that at the bottom of the letter he points out-and very courteously too-
I intend to discuss the case with Dr. Arnold shortly.
We will go a long way to meet your views.
I was waiting for a further reply. I might well have sent it across to the minister, but I thought it was a good document to illustrate my contention that at times the Board of Pension Commissioners and the officers of the Department of Soldiers' Re-establishment live up a little too much to the letter of the law;-I am endeavouring to be as moderate in my language as I possibly can, because I consider they have a difficult position, and I do not wish to make it more difficult. I know they have a very hard row to hoe, and I do not wish to make it any harder or to put this country in for millions of unnecessary expense. But I believe that in many cases the Board of Pension Commissioners and the officers of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment could give treatment or pension at not very great increase in cost to the people of the country, and give better satisfaction than has been given in cases such as the one I have mentioned. I make this statement in the House because

I wish to offer two other suggestions before I close, and I make these suggestions because the minister will present shortly recommendations of change in the Pension Act. I offer two suggestions which have been put up to me by a returned officer, which, I think, are very good suggestions, and which I think might possibly be dealt with by the minister when bringing in his amendments to the Pension Act.
He pointed out that if the widow of a man who was killed at the front is receiving a pension and she marries again, her pension automatically ceases. That is all right. He says: "Supposing her second husband dies within a reasonable time, she does not get a pension again," and he points out that in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, which is on the statute books to-day, even in such a case as that a woman on application would have an opportunity of being replaced on the pension list. I have thought the matter over, and I can see no real argument against the same condition being applied to the Pension Act in the case of the widow of the man who has served overseas. This would appear to me to be a just request. He quotes the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, section 56, subsection 2, and I will quote it:
If the widow remarries, her pension shall be suspended from the day following that of her remarriage. If in the event of her again becoming a widow her pension may be restored if she is otherwise qualified.
I quote that for the information of the minister. That is a suggestion that should, at least, receive consideration.
The other case, which to my mind is more unjust, I have taken up in this House before. It is the case of a woman who lived with her husband, a returned man, *who is seriously injured, and who is receiving a pension because of his injuries, or she and her family are receiving pensions because of his injuries. He for some reason-let us suppose it is because he gets into trouble with (the police-leaves the country. He does not dare to come back, or for some reason he does not come back. He deserts her; no matter what the reason may be; he

leaves her at any rate. Because he does not return at the end of six months and appear before the medical board to be examined, her pension and that of her children are cut off, the idea being that since the man does not return,-it is not a permanent pension, according to the expression used by the minister and therefore it is cut off. I believe some method must be worked out to do justice to women and children who are placed in that situation. I am sure it is not the desire of anybody in this country that the wife and children of a man who served overseas and who was seriously injured over there should suffer, if we can possibly prevent that, even at a great deal of expense to this country. I want to lay that case before the minister in order that he and his officials, when he brings in these amendments, may consider the possibility of bringing in some amendment to cover such a case as that.
Those are all the suggestions I have at the present moment. I did not mean to speak quite so long; but I have laid the facts before the minister because they are of great importance, and I hope they will be of some benefit to him and his commissioners and to the men who went overseas and their dependents.

It seems to me that we should have the most generous treatment possible as regards the returned men. It is not necessary to go into the recommendations of the pension commission. The returned men feel very strongly on this matter, and I think they have just ground for feeling that their cases have often not received from the present board the consideration that is due to them. This command views with great dismay and surprise the action of the Board of Pension Commissioners with reference to the report of the first part of the investigation into pensions made by the Royal Commission on the charges made by the Great War Veterans' Association. In view of the conduct and attitude of the board, indicating that it does not intend to carry out the administrative recommendations of the Royal Commission and in view of the previous mental attitude of the board, which shows, combined with its present conduct, that it is unfitted to administer the Pension Act,

The question before the committee is, perhaps, one of the most important matters which could engage our attention this session. It is important because it relates to a time when very strong and passionate emotions were aroused during the war, and appeals, such as we have not listened to for many years, were made to the manhood of Canada to respond to the call of their country and to place their all on the altar of this Dominion and of this Empire. Almost nine years have passed by since the commencement of that terrible conflict; five years have passed since the war has been concluded, and to-day we are still dealing with many of the pension cases, doubtful cases which, either by the administration of the Pension board or by the enactments of parliament, are found to be suffering an injustice. We are now, of course, considering pension estimates. There will come a time very shortly when the minister brings down his bill in amendment to the Pension Act, when we can discuss the concrete proposals for remedying the injustices and for arranging to adjust the many cases which have come before every member of this House.
In my observations of proceedings in this House during the past two years, it has seemed to me that on matters of this kind, a little too much apathy and a little too much reluctance has been shown by the members in taking the initiative as leaders of public thought in this country, and that soldiers' organizations and the public at large instead . have been obliged to stir up the members of

this House to bring about remedies and to force the appointment of a royal commission. Various reasons may be given for that. A parliamentary committee sat last year, and it my recollection is correct, all the recommendations of that committee were not carried out, although many should have been carried out at that time. What is the result? The result to-day-and it is a fact which no hon. member will deny-is that from Vancouver 'to Halifax there is dissatisfaction
on this	question	of	pensions,	on	theadministration of	the	act,	and	on	thestate of	the	law	as	we	find	it.
I do not think there is any hon. member in this House who will deny that statement: we are all receiving letters and resolutions of one kind and another advocating extreme measures to remedy the situation. What has been responsible for this dissatisfaction? In my judgment, the impression has got abroad -and that there is some truth in it, I do not doubt-that this dissatisfaction is due to a lack of sympathy on the part of the Board of Pension Commissioners. There is also an objection to the law as originally framed. When the act was passed there was established a principle that practically amounted to a contract between the soldier body of the country and the country itself, but the law has been so changed as to deprive many men or their dependents of the pensions they should otherwise receive. My amendments related to section 11 and section 25, subsection 3. given pensions on a different principle but one much less advantageous. In the reports a difference is made between what is known as the insurance principle and the "due to service" principle. So that after September 20 you find a line of demarcation. Before that day men and their dependents had a much greater opportunity of getting pensions than they have had thereafter. Last year, therefore, I asked the House and the government to accept the insurance principle, and to that end I moved an amendment to section 11 for the purpose of re-establishing the law as it was in 1919. Unfortunately, however neither the government nor the House saw fit to accept that amendment. The Ralston commission, after extensive investigation, has now brought down its report favouring the re-establishment of the insurance principle. My purpose in dwelling on the subject to-day is to urge upon the government and the minister not only the expediency, but the wisdom and justice-indeed, the sacred duty of themselves and of parliament-to adopt an amendment at this session to bring about this end.
I wish to call the attention of the minister to the fact that, in accordance with the report of last year, section 33, subsection 1, was amended in order to remedy an unfortunate evil which then existed. But the Senate rejected the amendment. This section as it stands to-day apparently prevents the payment of pensions to widows who were married subsequently to the appearance of disability causing death. The Board of Pension Commissioners has taken the stand that no latitude in the interpretation of the section is permissible. I would point out, however, that provision could reasonably be made in some instances where disability was incurred during service but did not become apparent until after marriage. I would also remind the House that a parliamentary committee during the session of 1922 recommended to the House a very satisfactory amendment to the section. The report of the committee was adopted and an amending bill to that end was passed in the latter part of the session. But the amendment was deleted in the Senate and the bill was referred back to the House and adopted in the form amended in the other Chamber. I trust that the minister on this occasion will remedy that situation.
I would call to the attention of the government their own obligation in connection with these different amendments and in relation to recommendations that have been embodied in the Ralston report. Prior to the election of 1921 the Great War Veterans' Association LMr. Ladner ]
submitted to the various leaders of the parties engaged in that contest specific questions which those gentlemen were asked to answer in order that the great soldier body might know to what extent the leaders and their respective parties would go if re-
5 p.m. turned to power. At that time the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was one of those who received these questions.' He made a general answer in which he gave expression to a statement the thought and sentiment of which finds great favour with me, and which I think creates an obligation on the part of the government that I trust they will realize and discharge at this session. Speaking at Cobalt on November 20. 1921, the right hon. gentleman is reported to have said:
" Our duty to the returned men, their dependents, and the dependents of those who have not come back, is clear," Mr. King stated. "It is a demand that we treat their requests with generosity, which is more than mere justice. To the men who sacrificed their all in the fight for. freedom we owe all the freedom we have to-day; though we default the interest on the national debt (which would mean national bankruptcy), we cannot afford to let one of our returned men or their dependents suffer."
That is a very fine and noble sentiment. But sentiment is not very useful to men and women in this country who are to-day walking the streets without the wherewithal to provide the necessities of life. The responsibility for improving this situation actually rests upon the government to-day, in view of the statement I have just quoted, and I suggest to the government and to the minister that, when the amendments to the Pensions Act are brought down, they remember their sacred pledge given on that occasion, and take advantage of the recommendations which have been made after investigation in the Ralston report. I trust that we may have amendments to the act which will do justice to the many cases, knowledge of which every member of the House has in his possession, which have not been provided for either because of some technicality in the law, or of faulty procedure in the administration of the act, or of some inefficiency in the department. I am not of course for a moment making any general charge in that regard. But there are instances where cases have been decided differently on the same set of facts.
I wish to take advantage of this occasion to offer to the minister some suggestions that have been made to me by different organizations. The first is that the pensions of orphans be increased from S30 to $45 per month. A number of organizations believe that increase is necessary, and I personally

Supply-S.C.R.-Pensions
think the additional expenditure involved would not be so serious as to weigh against the advantages which would accrue to the children by the increase. Another matter- I am citing these because they are not ordinarily reviewed in the discussion of this question-is this:	It is urged that provision
be made to meet the cost of burial of widows, widowed mothers and pensioned children. These requests have been submitted to the department, and I wish to urge upon the government the justice of accepting them; I know the minister is very sympathetic and will look into them carefully. Another question which can properly be considered here is one which was dealt with by the special committee on pensions last session, namely, the helplessness allowance for soldiers who have become totally blinded as the result of service overseas. These men, in addition to their pension, receive a helplessness allowance. Those who are able to go out upon the streets are in need of a guide. The practise of the department is to allow these men, I think, S25 a month or a little more, which is not sufficient to provide that necessary assistance, and the result is that when these men walk upon the streets-I know of concrete cases in Vancouver, they fall over wheelbarrows, trip over ropes and excavations where the streets are being repaired, and in general suffer many inconveniences and difficulties through their disabilities. Their complaint is best set out in the words of one of the men, Mr. A. Baron Taylor, in a letter addressed to myself, to which communications from some of these organizations are attached. He says:
I certainly think that we are entitled to at least two-thirds of the maximum-
The maximum is $75 a month.
-for it is acknowledged that blindness is the most pitiable of war disabilities, yet we receive less than one-half the maximum allowance, despite the fact that each may be blessed with trench foot pains or shattered nerves. I trust that I have made the situation clear on this point.
Another thing that vitally affects some of us is the fact that our wives, on becoming widows, receive no pension because of marrying after the disability was incurred. This, to me, is a gross insult to both parties concerned, for it immediately puts the sacred marriage on a commercial base and has the tendency to class the wife as a prostitute. Will you kindly remember these points when the debate reopens.
I consider it my duty to make a plea on behalf of these men who are suffering from this disability and for whom the helplessness allowance is not sufficient to provide the assistance they so much need.

Is it not a fact that the
helplessness allowance is $750 a year?
237J

That is the maximum,
given to a man, for example, who is blind and who has both arms off ot both legs off. That is a case where an attendant is required all the time, at the man's side; but when a blinded man is able to walk out upon the streets he gets only a portion of that allowance. My contention is that the purpose is to provide the necessary help for a blinded man to enable him to get along the street. I do not think the allowance should be cut in two simply bceause a man is able to walk outside instead of being always fed from a tray, and so on; the idea is to enable him to get along the street in comparative safety.

Has a certain scale been
established-so much for a walking patient and so much for a patient confined to the house?
Yes, they draw distinctions between certain classes of patients.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend not
think that a pensioner who receives $900 a year and besides that a helplessness allowance of $750 is able to provide someone to attend upon him in the house and accompany him when he goes out in the street?

Quite so, but that is not
the point of my contention.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I do not catch the hon.
gentleman's point, then.

The blinded man who is
able to walk along the street does not receive the full helplessness allowance of $750.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: He may receive it.

The information I have
is that he receives about $25 a month or slightly more. This man says in his letter that he wants to get a least two-thirds of the maximum. He ought to know-he is one of them.
What is his disability?

Total blindness; and he
is connected with some organization. He
says:
I certainly think that we are entitled to at least two-thirds of the maximum.
And so on. As I say, I understand they get about $25 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The helplessness allowance is left to the discretion of the Board of Pension Commissioners. As my hon. friend knows, it may be not less than $250 a year and not more than $750. It is for the board to judge what allowance should be awarded
Supply-S.C.R.-Pensions

to a man who is helpless on account of blindness. I understand they must award the maximum in the case of a man receiving the full pension of $75 a month, or $900 a year; that would bean additional $750 a year to enable him to have assistance in the house as well as outside. We have married men working in the department for $750 a year. I am sure it is possible for a full pensioner to secure the services that he requires when he receives the amounts I have stated, particularly when it is a case of not preparing his meals but serving them and accompanying him on the street. I may say that the regulations of the department provide for free transportation to totally blinded soldiers twice or three times a year. I am only stating the condition as it is; of course, my hon. friend may be able to suggest better treatment.

This matter was thoroughly discussed before the special committee of last year: I was not on the committee but I was present, and followed these points closely. The difficulty is that the board do exercise their judgment, but they exercise it on this basis: They say that if a man is totally blind and is not, for instance, able to look after himself at all-cannot get his food for himself but has to sit in a chair and have an attendant constantly waiting upon him- the disability is more severe than that of a blinded man who can walk outside and proceed along the street. They maintain that a man who can walk around the street, even though totally blind, should not receive the maximum allowance. Now, that is an argument; it is logical; it is a lawyer's argument. And the trouble with the Pension board is that they have carried logic and the law so far into their administration that injustices have resulted and do result. My suggestion is that what they should regard is not this relationship between one man who is totally incapacitated and another man who can walk about the streets, but the need that the man has in order to accomplish the purpose of his activities. For example in the one case he requires help to feed him. He has to sit down and he requires someone to look after him, and they pay him $75 a month. In the other case the man should have the right to walk about the streets even if it is necessary to pay two-thirds of the allowance or $50 a month as they say here, to get a child or somebody to guide him by the hand. The main consideration of the Pension board in that case should be the taking of the man on to the streets, and if they have to pay $50 a month to get someone to do it they should
IMt. Beland.]
pay it. In other words they have figured out the relationship between the two on the wrong principle. If the Pension board say that that is the legal interpretation, and they must persist in doing it and will not do it in any other way-and I have found them uncommonly stubborn in matters of that kind -what is the remedy? The responsibility is on the government and parliament to say: If you will administer the law that way, we will have to change our laws so that you will administer them in some other way. I am bringing this matter to the attention of the minister to-day because I certainly intend to deal with it later at another opportunity.
I would like before taking my seat to refer to one or two actual cases. A number of men have spoken of such cases, and it is a splendid way to illustrate the operation of the act. All of us have a great many of these cases. In this particular case I am not specially attaching any blame to the minister of the department, but I am attaching blame to the Pension board, and its administration, to its lack of sympathy. The facts show the need of certain amendments in the law. I have one case which I might cite by way of an example largely because the applicant is resident in Ottawa and the evidence was available in Ottawa. It is the case of Mrs. Florence G. White, whose husband died of malignant cancer at Christie Street hospital in Toronto, in July, 1921. It was a case of carcinoma, I believe the doctors call it. This man served overseas. He was a married man with a family. He went overseas and in June or July of 1918 he was shot down while flying over the German lines. In falling he was hurt somewhat. He was made a prisoner in Germany and I believe he had to eat many things there which in a number of other cases have been known to cause cancer. As a result of his experiences he came back to Canada and about the time of his discharge he returned to his position in the Marine department in this city. He came back to Canada in June, 1919, was discharged July 16, and returned to the Marine department August 6. At the time of his return to Canada he informed a number of people, responsible people whose word is worth something, that he was constantly suffering pain in the region of his abdomen where the cancer developed, and from a pull of the leg when he was going upstairs. The doctors of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment diagnosed it as appendicitis and treated this case of malignant cancer as appendicitis. They took him to hospital, and finally he had to relinquish his position with the department. First of all, he had taken a few days off from

Supply-S.C.It.-Pensions
his job, informing a high official in the government that he was constantly suffering from this pain and would like to be released. All these facts were sworn to in affidavits and filed with the Pension board. This man went to St. Luke's hospital in June, 1920, and the doctors of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment operated on him and found that instead of appendicitis he had cancer. They had to get consent before a subsequent operation could be performed, and he was sewed up temporarily and was later on operated on again and finally died. That was, of course, a case of attributability due to the change in the pension law.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: When did he die?

In July, 1921. We proved by a number of the very best witnesses you could possibly find all the facts that were relevant and were available to be proved, showing that the man suffered from pain, and the position, and everything absolutely dovetailed with the cancer pains which afterwards became more severe.	[DOT]
Was he discharged as fit or unfit?

I do not know the exact
category in which he was discharged. At any rate, I believe reference was made in one of the reports to the pains1. Of course, the pains might have been something else. After this the case was1 presented to the Board of Pension Commissioners, but unfortunately all the facts which a lawyer would know were relevant and pertinent to proving the case were not given to the Pension board. The matter was brought to my attention and I got affidavits and prepared a statement of the case and placed it before the board. I found that' the board refused to reconsider their position, and I also found out as a lawyer of some years' experience in my practice the real procedure that the Pension board carried out and the reason why a great number of injustices have been done in this country. You have on that board a lawyer, a doctor or two doctors, and somebody else. I laid the evidence before this body which exercises final judicial authority. I said: There are the facts for the plaintiff's case, here you have the facts for the department; now on what grounds do you refuse to reconsider this case? On one particular point on which three different people swore to a fact which bore directly upon the case, one of the commissioners said to me, "Why, Mr. Ladner, that is not so." I said: "How do you know it is not so?" He replied: "As a doctor I know that things like that practically never happen." He took the inference of his medical
mind to perform the duty of a judicial mind, with the result that he simply refused to listen to anything in the way of these facts sworn to in the affidavits and said, "In my opinion this did not happen." It appears that carcinoma or cancer does not often happen from a blow but from some other cause, but it might easily have happened in Germany when he was a prisoner there. But the board refused to reconsider the case. I then took all the facts and a new statement of the case and placed it before the pension section of the parliamentary committee of last session. Some hon. members present will remember the case. We had quite a heated discussion. We had present Col. Thompson, Dr. Burgess, Mr. Paton and a number of other officials. The evidence was all gone over again, and I pointed out that the board were in fact exercising a judicial function and that they should carry out their duties in accordance with established principles of evidence, that they should not go by inference, guesswork or medical theories, but by the evidence before them, and on that score we had the evidence. The committee on pensions appreciated that point and came to the decision that the board was wrong and that it should reverse its finding and grant the pension. A communication was formally sent to them but the medical member of the board said "We have made up our minds on this case and we are going to stick to it, we will not change." Now, in my opinion, as a lawyer of some years standing and practice before the bar-having heard the members of the committee discuss this case, having seen the prepared evidence- we actually had the applicant, her mother, her son and another witness present before the committee to give verbal evidence and be subject to a cross-examination if desired-in my opinion the committee absolutely failed, and the Pension board absolutely failed, to cany out the fundamentals of judicial procedure; and in that respect I must commend the minister for suggesting in the resolution he has brought forward that something in the nature of appeal boards should be provided to which people such as this applicant can go, so that their whole life's work and interest shall not be finally determined by somebody who obstinately clings to his own view of the case. Take the case of a Chinaman in the matter of an ordinary contract or debt or the case of an ordinary vegetable man out West and there is a contract involved of, say, SI.50, why that man can go to the Supreme Court of Canada and there are at his disposal the finest trained judiciary of the country, and all the common law precedents,
