and he can have justice. But when a case goes before the Pension board it is pronounced upon by men some without legal training. They come to their conclusion and whatever reasons to the contrary are advanced those reasons are overborne and it is hopeless to do anything further for the applicants. In that respect I for one am frank to say that I would like to see a change in the law by which it would be possible to get justice done outside the Pension board as it is administered to-day.
In this case,:-the White case-what were the consequences? This lady is a widow with a child at school. She had had two serious operations. She was denied by the doctors the right of carrying on her occupation as a nurse, she had no other means of earning a livelihood, she had to take her son from school and put him to work and she herself had to earn whatever she could. The husband in this case gave his life for his country, and yet the son is denied the opportunity of getting the education which he otherwise might have got. So that in the administration and practices of the Pension board we not only have the actual consequences of a pension not being paid, but also the effects of that action upon the families concerned for a generation and perhaps two generations to come. Now, Mr. Chairman, there are other cases that I might cite but I will merely mention the names because the particulars are all on file. There is the case from Vancouver of Captain H. A. Langford in which all the particulars have been placed before the department. There is another case, that of E. N. Couch, living in South Vancouver, which is quite involved and which depends largely upon the question of attributability.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that the question of pensions is a matter which should engage the attention of every single member of this Hous'e. I do not believe that we as members have the right to feel any apathy with respect to it, and I hope that when the amendments to the Pension Act come down they will contain practically all of the recommendations that are embodied in the Ralston report, and that a means will be found of rectifying the injustices Which have been disclosed in the actual administration and in the procedure of the Pension board.

I shall be very brief in my observations to the committee at this time, but at a later date when the amendments to the Pension Act are discussed I may have more to say. I suppose that Canada has been a little negligent of the welfare of her returned soldiers. In this respect history is only repeating itself. That seems to have
rMr. Ladner.]
been the case in all countries and after all wars. Nevertheless in comparison with othet countries and with other periods, I think Canada, perhaps, has a good record. Still, I believe there have been some cases of injustice, and perhaps that is to be expected
The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) has referred to the position of the Pension board. I can understand that in dealing with returned soldiers distributed all over Canada, and receiving reports from a great distance and from doctors whom the board does not know, and some of whom are very persistent in advancing claims on behalf of their patients, the board feel that they must be very firm in order to protect the country from being imposed upon. In the constituency I have the honour to represent there are no very large centres of population, and perhaps, that is the reason why very few specific charges against the board have reached me. Yet in a general way there have been several complaints, and i: would certaiply seem that there are a goodly number of men who have not been well treated. It seems rather sad too when such a spectacle as was witnessed by the people of my own town last week occurred. That was the sight of two returned men, each of whom had lost a leg, on their way at the present time from Calgary to Ottawa in order to lay their complaint before the proper officials there.
Reference has been made to the fact that during the last few years the reins have been somewhat tightened, but that, I think, is only to be expected. I do not think we can attribute the fact to the change of government. The same thing has occurred in connection with the Soldier Settlement board. Having been imposed upon in the early years of their history it is quite natural that the pendulum should have swung in the other direction and, perhaps, swung too far. Probably that is what has taken place in connection with the Pension board. I should like to say that I have received several telegrams in which the desire is expressed that the recommendations of the Ralston commission be put into effect. I think if I read a few words from one of these communications it will express what is conveyed in the others. I find in one telegram these words:
To get immediate action taken which will give effect to the findings of the Royal commission, as we have in this province a large number of urgent, necessitous cases affected thereby.
I only wish to say further in connection with the returned soldiers-particularly those who are maimed or crippled-that while it is

Supply-S.C.R.-Pensions
time that Canada practise every economy I do not think this is a direction in which it should be done. I should like to see the most generous treatment towards these men- in fact the treatment should be very generous before I could demur in any way to the expenditure for this purpose.

This, perhaps may be the appropriate time to interject a remark or two of a slightly different tenor regarding the operations of the Pension board-and I may add the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment as well. Everybody's judgment, to be of any value in cases of this kind, must be based on observation; and while for the last three years I have had a very considerable number of cases to take before these two boards I am very much pleased indeed this afternopn to be able to state unreservedly to the House, that not only have I received from them the most courteous treatment and prompt consideration but my experience has been that they have leaned always towards a sympathetic interpretation of the law. I can only say what I have found myself. In the last week I had occasion to take up a case with the Pension board, and there was some doubt in my own mind as to how they should act. Greatly to my delight, and somewhat to my surprise, the matter was settled almost immediately. A telegram was despatched to my constituency conveying certain instructions, and the claims of the applicant were met and met very promptly.
I would hold up both hands for any change in the act which would give a more generous treatment, if possible, to our returned men, and I would support unreservedly any features of the Ralston report which have that end in view. I wish to say that none of the criticisms which have been levelled against the administration of the Pension board in my opinion is well grounded. This may not be a popular view to express; I know that a great many people take a different view. Many associations of soldiers seem to imagine that they are receiving entirely unsympathetic treatment. I can only judge by what I know, and I have not found that to be the case. The same remark applies to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. I have carried some appeals to that body to a successful conclusion and in a manner that gave me satisfaction. Most of my work in connection with the Soldier Settlement Board has been carried on through the secretary, Mr. Paton, and I have found him an efficient officer. He has been always most obliging, and has rendered me service auite equal to that which I
could reasonably expect from any government official of any department. I would like to see the act enlarged in any possible way that will give better and more generous treatment to those who so richly deserve it, but I do not like to have this discussion closed without saying a word in commendation of men whom I have found to be very efficient and courteous.

Numerous complaints which
have been forwarded to members of parliament during the course of the last two or three years must, I am sure, have been received with some sense of apprehension. I believe that it was for the purpose of securing finality in connection with pension problems that last year this parliament authorized a twofold investigation; an investigation first for the purpose of inquiring intc certain definite charges made, and, secondly, for the purpose of investigating, examining and figuring out the best possible way to meet any grievances that might exist.
In this connection I am satisfied that the people of Canada desire that the fullest justice should be done to the returned soldiers. I think that the people of Canada, too, have some reason to be grateful to the soldiers' organizations which have brought before the public at large the questions involved. I think that Mr. MacNeil, who has given so generously of his time and of his efforts, deserves the thanks of the people of Canada for bringing, as he has ably done, before the commission the consideration of various problems which were under their purview.
With regard to the first part of the invest! gation, it appears that the Ralston commission have found the charges well-founded, except in so far as the charges covering the matter of conspiracy and lack of good faith were concerned. With regard to the second part of the report, I regret that it has not been distributed so that it is impossible to know, except from newspaper reports, the nature of the recommendations which have been made. I am hopeful-and I am sure the minister in presenting his pensions recommendations to the House, will see to it- that these will have as their purpose the desire to give the fullest justice to returned soldiers. I am satisfied the people of Canada will be satisfied with nothing else. We need, I think, speed and efficiency in consideration of these problems. We need justice in their disposition. It occurs to me that, perhaps, something may be accomplished if we strive for, not only simplification of the work of the pension department, but also unification. I
Supply-S.C.B.-Pensions

have been somewhat surprised by the formula through which the pension applicant must go before he can have his case determined. I do not know whether it has occurred to the minister-I presume it has-but it seems to me there should be some method by which these two principal organizations that we have now, the Pension board on the one hand and the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment on the other, might well be placed under one head, in order that the work might be co-ordinated, and that there might be greater speed. I think this might assist, to some slight extent in securing the justice which the people of Canada desire should be given to every pension applicant. I propose to have something further to say when the legislation comes before the House.

What percentage of those
who are blind receive the full allowance of $750 per annum?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am not in a position to supply the information as to the exact number of blind soldiers who receive the full amount but I would think a large majority, if not all, receive it. I must congratulate hon. members first of all upon the moderate tone which has prevailed during the discussion. It was expected indeed that the discussion would be conducted in that spirit.

Is it intended to
close the discussion with the minister's remarks?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: My hon. friend might speak now. I would rather wait till all the members have expressed their views before I sum them up, as it were, and indicate what the action of the government is likely to be.

I will make a few remarks in this connection, but when the legislation comes up I desire to speak more fully. I think I am speaking as one who perhaps has dealt with more cases than most individual members in the House. I hold in my hand the papers relating to the cases I have dealt with during this session. I think the bundle of papers I have here would be a. fair representation of the work of one member with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. These cases cover exservice men from California to the Yukon and from the Pacific to the Atlantic. There may be one reason why I, perhaps, receive more applications than other members, and that is the fact that I was largely in touch with the medical work at the front. The number of cases will speak for the work of the board.

I am not out to "knock" the board altogether. I can criticize it and criticize it severely, but I doubt if you could get any other board that would do any better, because one of the most difficult duties I know of, connected with the administration of any department of the government is the endeavour to give satisfaction, to the exservice men.
I would like to bring one or two matters to the attention of the minister to-day and the first is the difficulties in connection with these cases. Eighty per cent of these cases of complaint are due to poor presentation of the case at the beginning. The ex-service man has had some medical officer, who is not thoroughly acquainted with ex-service conditions or with, the pension system in general to deal with his case. In these cases I find that the large majority of the difficulties are due to a poor presentation of the case at the beginning. Can the board or department escape criticism in connection with these cases? I do not think they can, because my criticism of the board is, perhaps, largely lack of sympathy, that they do not assist a man in the presentation of his case. Let me exemplify that in one or two cases.
I came in touch with an ex-service man named Dumais, who had cancer in the pelvic region. He received no assistance whatever from the board. When I met the man I said to him: "Have you any history of sickness during your service?" "No, nothing whatever; I was never in a hospital during my service." "Have you any history of an injury?" "No." I said, "Think." He said, "I never thought of it before; during my service a horse kicked me exactly in this place, and I lay in my lines for three days without making any report." It seems strange that during all this time no person in the department suggested to him the history of an accident. Unfortunately that man died six days after I spoke to him. He had no relief; he had no benefit whatever. I am positive that the history of that man's cancer began with the injury he received on service. That is only one of a number of cases in which the board failed, and in those cases they failed to sympathize with the men's condition.
Let me give another example where, I think, they have fallen down and where any board might fall down, but I am giving this as a practical illustration how they can pull up on those cases. There is in the city of Kingston a man who has a history of illness, gas and so on all through the service. This man is now in a mental condition. He drives a cart. He gets off the cart and the

Supply-S.C.R.-Pensions
cart goes one way and he goes the other. That mental condition, I am satisfied, is due to the man's service and conditions affecting him overseas. He may have been in a slightly demented condition before; but he was accepted in that condition, and he went overseas. What did the department do? They were not satisfied as to the report of the medical officer at Kingston; and bear in mind that there are eight or nine medical men there. If they are not fit to carry out their duties, they should be removed and somebody else put in their place. That has been done lately; but that is not a criticism. They took this man from Kingston to Toronto, and they put him before a man who examined him for one day, and who said: "There is nothing wrong with that fellow," and the only explanation given to the man or rather to his wife is: "Cannot you go out and work and help?" That is the land of sympathy that men are getting in some cases from officers connected with the department.
There is a third criticism that I have of the board. A man who has a slight disability comes before them; they, perhaps, pension him along for a while, and later on they may bring him up before one of those specialists they speak about. They say to the man: "We will give you $200 to settle your case." That is ridiculous, and it is the harshest way of dealing with a man that I know of. They are simply trying to clear off the country's responsibility to this man by paying him $100 or $200. If a man has a disability at all, his pension should continue with that disability. If he has no disability, he should be told that he has none, instead of an effort being made to buy him off. That sort of thing has been done too much by both governments, and I am not going to criticize one government more than the other. When the man was discharged he was brought up for examination and one question that was put to him was "Are you satisfied?" They expected to clear off the responsibility of the government or the state or the country to that ex-service man by the answer to that question. Fortunately that has fallen down. The department, however, are doing the same thing to-day; they are trying to buy men off with $100 or $200, because they think these men have no disability at all. They should be straight and above board with these men and meet them and say: "You have no disability; we are representing the state in this matter; we have no responsibility in your case, and therefore we are going to discharge you."
Is the hon. gentleman not aware that commutation of pensions was brought in at the request of the soldiers' organizations and in spite of the Pension board some two or three years ago?

I am not going to accept that as a reason for buying off a man.
I do not care who brought this in, whether it was soldiers' organizations or anyone else. My contention is that this is not a fair way of dealing with a man. Commutation of pension is a different thing altogether from giving this trivial pittance to a man to buy him off. A man may commute his pension; that has been done, and the country has suffered because a man has come back afterwards. That, however, is a different question. What I am speaking of is the effort to buy a man off saying: "Sign this and we are done with you." He may come back later on, ani they put this document up to him and say "You signed this and we are done with you.
These are two or three difficulties with which I have to deal in connection with cases that have come before me. I may say that I have secured satisfaction for ex-service men in 70 per cent of the cases with which I have had to deal, and that is pretty fair dealing; but in all of those cases the board had decided against the man in one way or another. When the case was properly put up, this requiring the work of a medical man to go thoroughly over the case, review it and bring it to a certain point, the man would get reasonable consideration; but this is work that, perhaps, somebody else should not have to do. All the same, I criticize the board along the lines I have mentioned but I doubt if any other board would do any better.
On the other hand, we have just as many criticisms with regards to people who are receiving pensions but who are not entitled to them and for that reason we should be very careful not to throw the board down so that the state or the country may suffer. What we want is a fair deal, a good honest board. What is my recommendation to this end? It is that if you want satisfaction in these cases, you must have men who can give you satisfaction, and I do not believe the medical men doing the work to-day are big enough for the job. You must go out and get the biggest men in the country and pay them decent salaries. If you do that, I think the country will be satisfied and will say: "Well, they have done all they can anyway to meet these men." I know men are on the board for service overseas and so on; but the biggest medical men in Canada were overseas

and I think their services could be secured. You must make sure that you get big enough men to deal properly with the questions that are brought before them by doctors from the smaller places, and you must pay them reasonable salaries. That is my main criticism, and I think this criticism that comes from many centres will be met if you secure big men as advisers to the board and pay them reasonable salaries.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I have just a few words to say with regard to the item before the committee. I am fully aware of the very difficult position which the Pension board occupies. The members of this board have to consider very many serious cases, a number of which I have cognizance of myself. I agree with the remark of my hon. friend who spoke this afternoon (Mr. Ladner), that if the board is a judicial body it does not always act in a judicial manner. Numerous cases come before the board for consideration, and I have noticed within the last year or so that it has been becoming increasingly difficult for any man to get consideration at their hands. I am not in any way adversely criticising the board, but there are a few discrepancies in the act which I think the present minister might very well take into consideration.
I want to submit two or three cases that show that in some cases the board has been somewhat unjust to pensioners. I would refer the minister first of all to pensioner No. 666,734 who had a permanent disability of five per cent recorded on initial examination. This meant a pension for himself and family of $7.50 a month. On September 28, 1920, he was informed by the board that he could have his pension commuted to a lump sum of $300 in cash. This, of course, is not a large amount, in comparison with the enormous sums which this House considers at various times but it is nevertheless of considerable significance to the individual who gets it. In this case the complaint is not in regard to the meagreness of the amount involved, but the apparent injustice that has been done the pensioner. The sum of $300 was allowed him as a commutation for a five per cent permanent disability pension. I wish the minister clearly to understand that the disability was recorded as permanent. This man decided that he would not commute 
the pension but would continue to draw $84 per annum or thereabouts instead of taking the single payment of $300. In 1922, in the month of January, or eighteen months afterwards, he was summoned to Toronto, where he was examined, and was informed that his disability would be reduced to three per cent Naturally, he was very much surprised at this, because his discharge papers distinctly showed that he had a five per cent permanent disability. The fact, however, was that the disability was reduced to three per cent and he was told that he would be given a ca*h payment of $75 and be discharged. Now, the man was not at all unfair. He said he would be perfectly willing, if the board would grant it, to accept the balance to make up $300. He stated to the board that he had refused the commutation of $300 in the mistaken belief that he had a five per cent permanent disability which would entitle him to a pension for the rest of his life. The matter was taken up by the board who granted him another hearing in Toronto; and that second board confirmed the previous decision reducing the disability to three per cent. I had the man examined in Milton by local doctors who gave him a certificate of over five per cent disability. But the board came to the conclusion that local men did not understand the case. They therefore decided to appoint a man of their own in Toronto, a specialist named Clarence Starr, who examined the pensioner and gave him a certificate of between five and ten per cent, thus increasing the amount of disability which he had in his favour in the first instance. The matter was then placed before the board for ie-consideration. After considering it, they decided that the initial examination on which the man was granted five per cent permanent disability, carrying the commutation award of $300 in cash, was wrong. They refused any relief. This is a case in which the board absolutely refused to accept the certificate of independent medical men who examined the man, and rejected the certificate of their own appointee in Toronto, a specialist, I might almost say, of national standing. The point I want to impress upon the minister is this: Instead of basing their decision on the evidence submitted to them, they acted, so to speak, as witnesses in their own behalf and gave a verdict on their own evidence. They were not fair to the man in refusing to accept the independent evidence submitted to them, and in constituting themselves, not, as they were in fact, a judicial body, but witnesses in a cause.

I have another case to bring to the attention of the minister; the regimental number is 438489. I do not make any statement against the board in regard to this case, which is a very unfortunate one. It is that of a soldier who went overseas, served in the Canadian Expeditionary Force during the whole war, came back to the city of Port Arthur and took ill there in the summer of 1922. There was no possible way of connecting his illness with his service; at least they could get no evidence to connect it. The point is that this man was suffering from cerebrospinal meningitis of infectious origin. In fact, it was stated to be of syphilitic origin. He was sent to an asylum in Toronto and his w'ife was left penniless in Port Arthur. She was sent down to her sister in the county of Halton; that is how the case came to my attention. The sister was the wife of a returned soldier who had no means of supporting this woman; he was on a small farm which he had purchased under the federal land settlement scheme. The woman was dying of tuberculosis. Both these persons have since died, and they received nothing whatever from the government to assist them, although the husband had served during the whole of the war and the wife had gone to work in order to maintain herself in his absence. I must say that the Pension board has nothing to do with this case, but there is something wrong with the Pension Act or the Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment Act when it allows a pensioner and the wife of a pensiQner to depend on charity for their subsistence. This was a very unfortunate case, the wife dying of tuberculosis and the husband dying of syphilitic spinal meningitis, having previously been dependent entirely on charity.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I may point out that under clause 12 of the act the board has discretion in such a case to award a pension if the soldier or his dependents are in a dependent condition.

I took this case up with the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment board here in Ottawa and also with the Pension board. I pointed out the peculiar circumstances in which these people were situated, and directed attention to the fact that they had failed to get any assistance whatever. The Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment board claimed that he did not come under their jurisdiction and that they could do nothing in the way of treatment, and the Pension board absolutely refused to grant a pension. They said the matter did not come under
their purview; that they were unable under the Pension Act to give any assistance to this very dependent wife who, suffering from tuberculosis, was dying at the time. I cannot quite understand the statement of the minister, having regard to statements of the Pension board in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I may say in this connection that the department has treated and is treating now many soldiers suffering from syphilitic affections. That is so far as the department is concerned; so far as pension is concerned, naturally that would come under the Pension board. I will read to my hon. friend section 12 of the act:
A pension shall not be awarded when the death or disability of the member of the forces was due to improper conduct as herein defined; provided that the commission may-
The commission "may".
-when the applicant is in a dependent condition, award such pension as it deems fit in the cir-cumstanees.
So the board has full discretionary power in a case of that kind to award a pension to the widow or to the wife of the soldier.

The case was placed squarely before the board, and they claimed that his disability was not due to his service, and that he was therefore not entitled to any pension; and the same was said of the dependent wife. Of course, they do not need it now; there is none of the family left.
Another case I wish to bring to the attention of the minister has to do with regimental number 663.242, pension number 106,363. This man served overseas as a private, returned, was rated as having a pensionable disability and was receiving a pension of S7 a month. He has not been able to do a single day's work since he returned toward the end of 1918: during all this time he has been dependent on his family. He had apparently a peculiar disability, one in connection with which no pathological change could be found. Having received his pension up to January, 1922, he was asked to go to Toronto for treatment. He remained in hospital in Toronto from January, 1922, until May 5, 1922, receiving treatment. He was then discharged from hospital; the doctor told him he could do nothing further for him. Shortly after returning to his home he was notified that his pension had been discontinued. In October I made a further application on his behalf and on October 9 he was returned to the hospital in Toronto for treatment. He remained there for four days, from the 9th to the 13th of October, when, claiming that he could not stand the treatment he was being given, he voluntarily left the hospital and went home.

A report was then sent in to the Pension board, but they still refused to reinstate his pension. I have taken the matter up with the board on several occasions and they maintain that this man's pension cannot be reinstated unless he submits to further examination and treatment. The claim is made that although this man has been under the doctor's care for over a year, there has been an absolute failure to diagnose his case and to establish any pensionable disability, although the Pension board admit that he is entitled to a pension. Simply because he refuses to return for examination and treatment he is prevented from drawing that pension. I have tried to prevail upon him to return for treatment and consideration of his case, but he refuses to do so, and consequently he is penalized on that ground.
For what reason does he refuse treatment?

Because, he says, the treatment he received has not done him any good and the treatment he received on the last occasion he was there was so severe that he was unable to stand it. He claims that when he left the hospital he was scarcefy able to walk owing to the pain which had been induced by the treatments given. His family now refuse to allow him to return. I think this is a case that might well be looked into by the minister and given serious consideration.
I have one other case to submit-and I may say that these are only a few of the cases which have come to my attention. A soldier who enlisted in 1914 was sent to Valcartier camp and was there only a short time when he contracted cerebro-spinal meningitis and was sent to hospital. During the attack of cerebro-spinal meningitis he contracted pneumonia. He was in hospital there during all the time the soldiers were at Valcartier, and for some time after they left. I cannot give his number; there was no record of his number or of his service; it was very difficult to find out anything about him so far as the records of the department were concerned. This man was a member of the 5th Field Company, Canadian Engineers. This is a letter from Mr. W. L. Malcolm:
He proceeded with us to Valcartier camp on or about August 16, 1914. While at the camp and while under my command Sapper W. L. Mullin contracted spinal meningitis, later followed by pneumonia. He was in hospital in Quebec for a very long period, being there after the camp at Valcartier had been cleared. Later I understood that he returned to Acton, but of his later movements I am not aware.
This man, then, had meningitis, on the statement of his commanding officer. When

this matter was first taken up before the commission, they declined to accept the evidence that was presented of spinal meningitis, but finally I got this letter from Colonel Malcolm. The letter is dated December 21, 1922, and says:
The history of meningitis while on service is not confirmed by records, nor at the time it occurred is there any record of there being a spinal meningitis epidemic. It is true an outburst occurred subsequently in the ranks of the C.E.F.
I remember distinctly hearing that there was an outbreak of spinal meningitis while the soldiers were at Valcartier camp. This does not agree with the statement of the Pension board, but later on apparently they got further evidence and they said:
This man enlisted on August 17, 1914. He took sick on September 24, 1914, at Valcartier camp and was admitted to hospital on the same date with a diagnosis of cerebro-spinal meningitis. He left hospital against the advice of the medical officer in charge and signed a waiver releasing the public from any responsibility for further care or treatment, or liability claim.
On that statement signed by this soldier the Pension board in the first instance based their statement that he was not eligible for pension. During the time after his discharge on the 15th of January, 1915, he was living in the town of Acton and was under treatment by a doctor there who has since died. There was a period of four or five years with no record of this man's disease from any medical officer so far as could be discovered. In 1921, on August 9, six years and seven months later, this man was taken very seriously ill. Previous to being taken ill he had been married, in 1918, I think it was. He had applied for life insurance, and when making his application for life insurance the examining physician discovered that he had a mitral insufficiency, that is a heart lesion, resulting as he said from endo-carditisr. In 1921, six years after this man's discharge, he had a very serious attack of endo-carditis. He was attacked with embolism and was examined by three physicians, and died after consultation. Application was made by his w'idow for a pension and each of these three physicians, well known in that vicinity, gave a certificate that this man died from cerebral embolism produced by heart lesion which they claimed was the result of cerebro-spinal meningitis suffered in 1914. This was brought to the attention of the board, but the board refused a pension on the ground that cerebro-spinal meningitis rarely if ever caused a heart lesion but they forgot that this soldier also suffered from an attack of pneumonia at the same time as he was stricken with spinal meningitis. Now it is a well-known fact that spinal meningitis is an infectious

Supply-S.C .R -Pensions
disease and that it sometimes results in the formation of pus, particularly about the ear. We know also that pneumonia very frequently results in impaired heart action, particularly pneumonia that results from some specific poison. After pneumonia, during an attack of la grippe, a heart lesion is quite frequent because pneumonia that results from a specific poison is not ordinary pneumonia, and it leaves the patient with an impaired and'faulty heart action which, if it is severe enough, may result in embolism causing sudden death. The minister will understand that. Cerebro-spinal meningitis we know from history rarely causes a heart lesion, that is endo-carditis, but it has been known to occur. These gentlemen of the board absolutely refused to accept the certificates of the three medical attendants who saw this man and refused a pension on the ground that his disability and his death were not due to anything that occurred during service, that his disability did not result from his service to the country and they claim that from 1915 when he returned home up to the time this disease was discovered by the doctor examining him for insurance there is a period of something like five years as to which there is no evidence that the man suffered from anything. But the point is that the doctor who attended him during those years is dead, and we cannot present evidence for that period, but there is the evidence of the three medical gentlemen who attended him at the time of his death. The doctors of the Pension board, who never saw this man, and who knew nothing about the circumstances except what is furnished by the evidence, refused to accept that evidence as a judicial board and say their own deductions are better than the opinions of the man who saw this case.
Those are the points I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. I think the board at the present time is not giving the soldier that sympathetic consideration and treatment which parliament intended when the act was passed. They are entirely dependent upon a technical reading of the act. They are administering the letter of the law and missing its spirit, and 1 think if there is anything needed by which these men could see their duty a little more plainly, if these little technicalities were removed from the act, it would be much more easy for the Pension board and a great deal more satisfactory for the soldier, particularly the man who desires to get consideration some time after his discharge from the army on account of a disability appearing after his discharge.
There is one other point I wish to bring to the consideration of the minister and it
is this: Many of these men were discharged from the army without a proper medical examination, and many of them were discharged as physically fit - who had some disability resulting from war service and which is unknown to the department. They were, of course, naturally anxious to get to their homes, and they did anything to get away, waived examination and allowed themselves to be called medically fit. and then later on when they returned to civil life they found they were not physically fit. Just as this man did at Valcartier. He was in a hurry to get home and signed this waiver releasing the country from all liability in regard to him. He came home and died, I think, as a result of his war service.
There is another peculiar feature about this case which .1 wish to bring to the attention of the minister for his consideration. The difficulty was to prove that this man's disability was due to war service. If we proved that his death was due to his military service but that his disability was known previous to his marriage, that entirely eliminated the widow from any chance of getting a pension. That question was brought up in the House more than a year ago, and we amended the act at that time to alter that condition in the Pension Act, but I understand that the amendment was thrown out in the Senate; at least I am so informed, I do not know whether it is correct or not. But after looking over this case and trying to convince the board that his death was due to service, I tried to bridge that gap between 1915 and 1921. I finally did find a doctor who had seen him during this period, and I got a certificate stating that he had examined this man- he was not sure of the date-and had found that he had an endo-carditis and valvular lesion of the heart. I placed the case before the Pension board, and they said that as the man's ailment was known previously to the marriage and that the woman married the man although aware of the fact she was not entitled to come under the provisions of the Pension Act; therefore she cannot get a pension. If such is the case I wish the minister particularly to consider that point, and to have the law amended so that a widow with a small family under such circumstances may be assisted in her own name.
In other respects I may say the Pension board have treated me with the utmost courtesy, and I have no criticism to offer excepting this, that I think they are adhering entirely too closely to the technicalities of the law, rather than interpreting the law according to the spirit. Not only should they interpret the law in a liberal manner, but
Supply-S.C.R.-Pensions

they should give the applicant the benefit of the doubt and not throw the onus of proving the claim entirely upon the returned soldier. Over and over again the board have stated that where evidence can be produced to show the man is entitled to a pension they will consider his case, but until proof of that can be submitted they will not grant him a board. I do not think it is the soldier's place to do that. I think that when a returned soldier, believing he has a disability, makes application for a pension it is the duty of the commissioners when that case is brought to them, to look into the matter and grant a board to inquire into the circumstances, thus deciding for themselves whether he is or is not entitled to a pension. Certainly the onus of proving the claim should not rest upon the returned soldier.

A great many cases have been submitted to the Pension board which we, from our viewpoint, regard as very reasonable. Some of these cases have received attention but others have been overlooked. I have in mind the case of a big, strong, healthy young man who went overseas, was wounded in the thighs and back and is now receiving the small pension of $11.50 per month. Shortly after his return home his eyesight began to fail and to-day he is totally blind. The case of this man has received attention from the board. He has been taken to Halifax and has undergone different examinations, but still the Pension board seem to be of the opinion that his blindness cannot be attributed directly to his overseas service. His claim for an increase in pension has therefore been turned down. This is one very outstanding case among a large number that I have been written to about, and I wish to thank the minister for the splendid assistance he has given me. In some cases, as I say, we have been able to get the pension claims adjusted. In other cases if we have not been equally successful the minister has done everything in his power to meet the situation. The board seem to act strictly according to the letter of the law, and, as has been stated here by different speakers, seem to evidence a lack of sympathy in some cases. Possibly we cannot blame the board for this as it may be their duty to act strictly in accordance with the provisions of the act. Nevertheless, I feel that in some cases such as I have mentioned there ought to be a means of redress; and I certainly hope that the appeal board that is to be appointed will give proper attention to deserving cases which everyone feels should

be thoroughly looked into. The blind man to whom I have referred has a wife and two children. I have a letter on my desk with respect to the case, but perhaps it would not be fitting at the present moment to take up the time of the House by reading it. Let me say that the people of the vicinity have had to go round and collect subscriptions to help this man and his family. It may be as well to point out that this poor fellow risked his life in our behalf. He is certainly deserving of greater consideration than he has yet received, and I trust that his case will be suitably dealt with.
I have also in mind another case. It is that of a woman whose two sons were killed overseas. Shortly afterwards her husband died. Although she has been left what we call a fairly good farm down in our province she is unable to work it, and derives no profit from this source. Her case has also been looked upon by the Pension board as not deserving of any consideration owing to the fact that she owns this property. I merely wish to put myself on record as saying that I trust that in the future such cases as these will be given greater consideration. I again thank the minister for his courtesy in assisting me in the great many cases I have brought before him.

During the discussion this afternoon we heard a great deal of criticism with regard to the administration of the Pension Act. I have had some experience in presenting cases to the Pension board, and I have never undertaken a more difficult task than that of interpreting the law and presenting properly cases of applicants for pension. The member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) made some reference this afternoon to the medical services. Personally I think he touched upon the point which requires attention and which contains the only cure if a cure exists as the law stands, namely, that we must have the best medical men this country possesses to perform the work connected with the Pension Act.
In the Canadian Pension Act we have a clause which is different from the Imperial Pension Act, a clause which has given rise to the difficulty. I do not think I exaggerate when I say that nine-tenths of the complaints that have occurred in Canada have arisen under that particular section, namely, that in order to secure a pension a man's disability must be attributable to service. In Great Britain (if a man was discharged and had nothing on his medical history sheet which indicated that he had disability connected with his war service that was the end of it, and if disability arose in the future no attention was paid

Supply-S.C. R.-Pensions
to it. In our country the law is quite different. If disability arises subsequent to discharge, although there is nothing on the medical history sheet to indicate that the disability was in any way connected with service, if it subsequently transpires that that disability which has arisen is attributable to service then the man gets a pension. This is purely a medical question. The Pension board -I do not care who they are-must be largely guided, and in ninety-nine per cent of the cases must be bound, by the conclusions of the medical men who investigate that particular point as to whether or not the disability is attributable to service. Now, I venture to say that as long as there are service men alive in this country there is going to be dissatisfaction under the Pension Act, unless the country is prepared to wipe out that clause altogether and allow any man who has had service overseas to come in and claim pension when disability arises, whether it is attributable to service or whether it is not. If you are going to leave the clause in the act that it must be shown that the disability is attributable to service, there will be dissatisfaction in this country amongst service men just as long as there are service men alive, because each applicant will be convinced that his disability is attributable to service. We might as well recognize that. The Ralston commission has proposed a cure for this dissatisfaction, namely an appeal board. I hesitate to differ with the royal commission that has had the advantage of evidence taken from coast to coast, and has had months to consider the matter. I am judging now by some of the applications for my support that are made by various men in this country who want jobs as members of these appeal boards. The minister can readily understand that I will have no influence in having members appointed on these appeal boards. Some of the applicants I would not recommend to the minister, and others I would. I can readily see the position the minister is going to be placed in when these applications begin to pour in from all over the country for jobs in nine different districts as members of these appeal boards and as advocates for the returned soldiers. I do not think that scheme is going to be a cure. I regret to think that it is not going to be a cure. I recognize, however, the situation which has been described by every speaker and the difficulties which have arisen under this particular section, and I personally think the most effective remedy is to improve our medical service until we evolve a medical service that will be so efficient that mistakes
will be reduced to a minimum. I do not think we can eradicate mistakes, but we can minimize them. Now I am not criticizing the medical service in the country, because I think the officials are doing their utmost, but they are dealing with these cases every day, and they adopt the official attitude which one is bound to adopt when he is dealing with such cases day after day, and the sympathetic touch with the returned men is lost, and these cases are very often dealt with in such a way that they do not get to the root of the trouble, and do not really determine whether the case is attributable to service or not.
The minister has determined to establish appeal boards, and I would hate to think that I would have any influence in stopping anything that is going to be of benefit to the returned soldier or going to assist in eliminating or minimizing the dissatisfaction . that exists. We have a judiciary in this country which to-day is not overworked; in fact, every province in this country has been enacting statutes which have reduced the volume of work whch our judges throughout the length of the country have to do. For instance, there are county court judges in every county throughout Canada. If the minister is going to have an advocate appointed in each of the eight or nine districts to advocate the claims of returned soldiers, why can the advocate not go before one of the county court judges who has been appointed by the Dominion and advocate his claim? They will certainly receive considerate and sympathetic treatment before our judges, because I do not think any body of men that we could pick out in the country would be more sympathetic than these judges. I think we would get justice just as readily from them as we will from appeal boards which are established, and which, as I am bound to say, will take on a political flavour, which would be a very serious matter in the interests of the returned men, if political appointments are going to be made, and I do not see how it is going to be avoided.

Last year I think the
committee dealing with pensions made a recommendation to the House that an appeal board should be constituted at Ottawa, and I understand it has been constituted. Does the hon. member know whether anything has come of it?
I have never run into it.

speechtext:
Better ask me the question. I can answer it.

Many cases have been presented and I want to make concrete suggestions as to amendments to the present Pension Act. I will refer to two cases which I have brought before the Pension board, and will ask for consideration. I am perfectly satisfied with the decision of the board in both cases, but they have convinced me that the law is such that they cannot do anything. Members have complained that these men carry out the law. What would be said *of them, if they did not carry out the law? They are bound by the statutes we have passed. I think where these difficulties arise, and we have cases which are not provided for by law, it becomes our duty to bring in concrete suggestions by way of amendment, to meet these different cases. That is what I propose to suggest now in reference to these two cases. One of these is the case of a woman whose marriage certificate I have in my possession. She was married in England, in good faith, and came back to Canada with her husband. Her husband died and she made application for pension; but it then appeared that the man was previously married, and his real widow, who had a family also, made application for the pension, and the pension was granted to the real widow. Now . this is not an isolated case, although it is the only one I have in my possession, but it is the type of case, which undoubtedly should 'be provided for. The first widow would no doubt have been entitled to her pension, but there is no reason in the world *why the second wife should not be provided for in the act.
Mr. BELAND Would the hon. member suggest that the two widows should each receive a pension in this case? I am simply asking for the hon. member's opinion.

Decidedly, I would say so, provided there was no immoral conduct on the part of either; but it so happens in this particular case the country would not be required to pay two pensions, because the first wife has since re-married; therefore, she has lost her pension, and the pension is now being paid to no one. But it is impossible under the law as it now stands to pay the pension to the second wife or widow.
The other is the case of Private McPhail, of Brandon, who died in Vancouver a short time ago. He was taken prisoner during the war and received very brutal treatment. He was wounded in the eye, and did not receive treatment for it for many days after he was taken prisoner. He came back to Canada completely wrecked in health and without his eyesight. He died the other day, and

I have forgotten the nature of the disease from which he died, but in any case it was some six years after discharge. Up to the time of his death he was a 100 per cent pensioner, but having died more than five years after discharge his widow was not entitled to the pension, because the medical officers of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment maintain that the disability from which he died was not due to service. The old question of attributability comes up in this case as in nearly every case. So far as cases of this type are concerned, they can be met by an amendment to the Pension Act. I would suggest that where a man was a disability case to the extent of 100 per cent or even, perhaps, of less than 100 per cent, no matter how long after discharge that man died, his widow Should receive a pension, because this is exactly the same as though the man were killed in France in service. The mere fact that he happens to live five or six helpless years will probably make the widow's case the harder. Far better for the widow had the man been killed outright, even though she received the total pension if he died six years or ten years afterwards. That is a case that might be taken under consideration. I have forgotten the number of the section; but the period is five years now, and where a man is a disability to the extent of 100 per cent, that provision should be wiped out, and no matter how long after discharge his death takes place, the widow should receive the full pension.
Those are two concrete suggestions that T have to offer to the minister, and I also hope, before he decides upon the exact nature of this appeal board, he take the matter unde-very serious consideration, because I do not foresee clear sailing by any manner of means under that appeal board. In fact, as I say, as long as we have in our act the provision that a man must show disability due to service, we shall [DOT] have dissatisfaction in this country, at least just as long as any ex-servic-3 man lives.

I think the tone ol the discussion that has taken place to-dav is not attributable to anything in the estimate before the committee, which estimate is the ordinary vote of recent years to provide for payment of pensions; but the discussion is because of the interest which the public i i taking to-day in the whole question of pensions payable to members of the
9 p.m. Canadian Expeditionary Force and their dependents. During the waf promises were made to the soldiers that the disabled and their dependents and the de-

Supply-S.C.R.-Pensions
pendents of those who were killed would be cared for. I do not think the public has grown cold in the matter; I think the public had simply lost track of the situation until very recently and was not in touch with what was going on. In line with public sentiment that returned soldiers and their dependents who needed help should be helped, legislation to that end was passed. The legislation was intended to be generous; it went further than any previous legislation establishing pensions had ever gone. It was passed entirely on the insurance principle: that is, pensions were awarded for any disability incurred or aggravated on service; it did not matter whether the disability or death was due to service or not. In other words, the country insured the soldier against any disability incurred while on service, whether or not the service caused the disability. For instance, a soldier on leave might be run over by a tram car and injured or killed. That disability incurred during the period of his service would entitle him or his dependents to a pension just as much as if he had inhaled poison gas from the Hun trenches or been killed by a Hun bullet. The other principle of the two is that pension is payable only because disability is due to service, for instance, where a man was wounded or killed in action. The present investigation and interest in pensions are due to charges made against the Pension board by the Great War Veterans' Association. That association complained that in 1920 the "due to service" principle was introduced into the act on the recommendation *of the Pension board, who represented to the parliamentary committee of that time that this principle would apply only to the permanent force and to those serving in peace time, and not to the Canadian Expeditionary Force. But according to the Great War Veterans' Association, notwithstanding those assurances, the principle was applied to the Canadian Expeditionary Force men and their dependents as well. In support of that, T propose to quote briefly to the committee some of the findings of the Ralston Commission. This is set out at page 44 of the first report:
The 1919 Pension Act had reference essentially to those who had served in the war, and it included the few who remained in service after peace was declared, to clean up the debris of war. The permanent force was not included.
The 1919 act provided that pensions were payable on the "insurance principle," that is, for any disability incurred during service, although not "due to service", but it was intended, by the second proviso to section 11, that when peace was declared, Canada would go back to the "due to service" principle.
The Great War Veterans' Association claims that this *change was not to affect discharged Canadian Expeditionary Force men, as to disabilities or deaths connected with their period of service, while the Pension board contends that it was to apply to all deaths or disabilities occurring after peace was declared, whether of discharged Canadian Expeditionary Force men or those still serving.
The commission found that, in its opinion, the change was only to apply to those who continued in the service for peace time duty, and was not to affect discharged Canadian Expeditionary Force men as to disabilities or deaths connected with their period of service.
The representatives of the returned men thought that the change was not to affect discharged Canadian Expeditionary Force men or their dependents.
The representatives of the returned men asked, before the 1920 Parliamentary committee and elsewhere, whether the Canadian Expeditionary Force men or their dependents were affected by these amendments, and were told by representatives of the Pension board that they were not. They also undertook that if any further provision were necessary to safeguard the rights of these men and their dependents, it would be put in. The representatives of the Great War Veterans' Association accepted these assurances and the amendments were passed.
In view of the commission's conclusion as to the true construction and intention of the 1919 act, it can be said now that these assurances were not carried out because the saving clause section 29, construed literally, did not protect the rights which discharged Canadian Expeditionary Force men and their dependents had acquired under section 11 of the 1919 act, but only saved disabilities or deaths occurring before September 1,	1920, as to everybody, Canadian Expeditionary
Force or otherwise. After that date the new section 11 came into effect as to discharged Canadian Expeditionary Force men and their dependents, as well as to all others, and this meant that after that date, if the statute were interpreted strictly, two classes of cases which formerly had been dealt with on the "insurance principle" would be refused pension unless they could show that the death or disability was caused by military service.
These classes would be-
And very wide classes they are:
(1)	The dependents of those who died after September 1, 1920, even though the death was due to something which was incurred on service, and even though the deceased had been receiving pension for the very trouble which caused the death.
(2)	The discharged Canadian Expeditionary Force man who had a disability which could be shown to be connected with his period of service, but who could not show that his condition at discharge was serious enough to constitute a disability.
Then the commission in general find in favour of the charges made by the Great War Veterans' Association, that is as to anything important in the charges, and the commission recommend legislation that will re-instate applicants, including their dependents, in their rights under the original act of 1919. There can be no doubt, I think, that the Pension board, within recent years at any rate, has constituted itself too much a watchdog of the treasury. They have looked on applicants for pensions with too much suspicion. They have, I believe, sought opportunities to refuse applications rather than to bring them reasonably within the act.

I do not think that the government wishes them to act in that way; I do not think that either parliament or the public wishes them to do so. I think they have taken the wrong cue. In the investigation before the parliamentary committee last session, on which I had the honour to serve, it was plain to me, as I think it was to the members of the committee, that the Pension board was carrying out the letter rather than the spirit of the law, or the intention of parliament-either of this or of preceding parliaments; and it was quite apparent to me, and I have no doubf it was equally obvious to the committee generally, that the board would persist in its policy of carrying out the letter of the law in that way regardless of the recommendations of any parliamentary committee. I understand, from press reports, that it is more than likely they will also disregard the recommendations of the Ralston commission. I believe the board could very much ameliorate present conditions by a little give and take in their administration of the act. They have tightened up too much.
This afternoon the member for Vancouver South (Mr Ladner) referred with some particularity to a case that came before the committee last session. I refer to what is known as the Percy White case. That matter was practically retried before the parliamentary committee last year. The board was represented before the committee and the applicant and her witnesses also appeared. Both sides were fully heard, and after hearing them and seeing them face to face the committee recommended that the pension be granted, and advised the board that in their opinion it had been wrong in refusing the pension. Surely that was reason enough for the board to relent and grant the pension. I do not think they are quite so conscience-bound as to be unable to do so if they really wished to be fair. But notwithstanding the representation of the parliamentary committee they refused to reconsider the matter. I do not say that the Pension board is always unfair or intentionally unfair, but in that case at least one of the members of the board was downright and intentionally unfair to the applicant. There is evidence on the file today of such unfairness on the part of at least one of the members of that body. There is evidence of personal antagonism to the applicant, who was a widow in ill-health, penniless and with an infant child to support. It is plain from the evidence that this member of the board so far forget himself as to ignore all demands of fair play and of gentlemanly instincts and to place on file grossly unfair notations, having no bearing whatever on 
the merits or demerits of the application, gratuitously insulting, and calculated to prejudice the board against the application. There is no question about that; if they have not been removed, the notations are there yet to speak for themselves. I do not propose to detail the evidence that was given before the parliamentary committee in that case; it was gone into sufficiently by the hon. member for Vancouver South this afternoon. I can only say that a flagrant injustice was done and is being persisted in; and that is only one of a number of similar cases which have not been remedied.
This new ruling of the board under which they tightened up in their policy became known to the Great War Veterans' Association only some six months after it had been made. For some unaccountable reason the board kept that ruling practically secret at head office until finally it got out in some way not accounted for. The evidence before the Ralston commission is that the board did not know how that minute was ever communicated to any of the district offices. They did not send it out officially; it leaked out mysteriously. Fortunately, however, it did get out and the Great War Veterans' Association then became aware of the principle on which the board was acting. This was the state of affairs in the closing hours of the 1922 session of parliament when Mr. Mac-Neil, the secretary of the association, realizing that something desperate had to be done to wake up the public, parliament and the government, sent his famous telegram. The telegram, I think, was worded extremely; there was no reason to suspect the Pension board of a secret conspiracy, which was the effect of the telegram. But there was every evidence to warrant Mr. MacNeil in assuming that secret regulations were being made-and as a matter of fact had been made, and had been withheld from the public-under which the board was acting. He had to startle the government into attending to that piece of public business; and he did so, with the result that the Ralston commission was appointed. After many sittings, a very thorough investigation and the hearing of much evidence and of many witnesses, the commission submitted a finding entirely favourable to the Great War Veterans' Association, recommending legislation which, if enacted, will leave very little to the discretion of the board. They recommend the establishment of central appeal boards.
It goes without saying that the position of members of the board is a difficult and delicate one to maintain. I have had exactly

Supply-S.C.B.-Pensions
the same experience as many members who have already spoken on this matter have had. I am free to observe that in regard to the specific cases which I have submitted to the board I have received nothing but the most courteous and proper treatment. I have half a dozen cases pending now before them and I expect the same treatment. But there is no reason why any special pleader should have to go to the board. They should decide all applications on their merits. No member of parliament should find it necessary to go to the board; nor should any applicant for a pension have to enlist the services of a member of this House, no matter how willingly they may be given. It should be all in the day's work of the board. The condition should not exist wherein the Pension board refuses an application and then, because some member of parliament or some other agent pleads the case further, reverses its decision. The decision should be right in the first instance. When we hear of cases being refused simply because they have not been properly presented, whose fault is it? Surely it is not the fault of the applicant; it is the fault of the board. The board should see to it that the evidence is all properly submitted and that the case is finally and fully presented before they give their decision.
I might mention one astounding case I have now in hand of a man who went to the war as a volunteer. He was a strong, healthy man in every respect, a six-footer. He was hit in the arm with shrapnel; the arm was shattered and has since not been of any use to him. He was sent from hospital to hospital till the armistice came and he was finally sent to Canada. He did not want to go to hospital in Canada and in his hurry to get his discharge he told them to mark him A-I. The disability was apparent, however; the arm was stiff, as it still is; he cannot raise it above his shoulder and cannot lift anything. They discharged him A-l, and in various ways he managed to get employment until' the past winter when he was up against it. When I inquired of him I was astonished to find that he was getting no pension, I advised him to apply and he did so; but to my amazement pension has not been granted. I have not found out why; it may have been because of his eagerness to get his discharge. But it is such cases as these that are causing dissatisfaction. Although the act is not as perfect as it should be or as it can be, I think that a great deal of dissatisfaction could have been avoided had the board seen fit to adopt a more diplomatic attitude. On the contrary, they have in some cases
238J
adopted the most toplofty or infallible attitude; they could not err; they could not make' a mistake; what they said was the law and must stand. That attitude is not calculated, to make the administration of that department very popular. The people are becoming alive to the fact that legislation is necessary to meet the present state of affairs and to give the board power to do what they say they would like to do but are prevented by law from doing. When that legislation is finally framed and passed and becomes effective, there may not be much need of appeal boards; personally I hope there will not be at any rate. I must say I have not very much faith that relief will be afforded by a multiplicity of pension boards which, in effect, is the legislation recommended by the Ralston commission. They really recommend the establishment of a great number of district pension boards. If one pension board cannot do any better than it has been doing, I do not think nine or ten or twelve will bring about any greater degree of satisfaction. I have more faith in the judgment of courts of the land, experienced and trained as they are in the weighing of evidence and the administering of justice. Expense, after all, is not a matter to be very seriously considered if we can get satisfaction for the returned soldiers and their dependents. But in any case, before adopting in toto the recommendations of the Ralston commission, I would urge the government to take into account the suggestion which has been made to-day by other members as well as by myself, namely, that appeals from the decisions of the Pension board should go to the regularly constituted courts of the land, which, I affirm, are quite.' competent to deal with the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
First of alj, I should like to make clear the position the minister occupies with regard to the administration of the Pension Act. The Board of Pension Commissioners is constituted by a special clause of the Pension Act, and it is provided by that act that the decisions of the board shall be final. So that whatever may be the desire of any hon. member or of any member of the government; whatever may be the desire of the minister in charge of the department, to whom the board is bound to make a report, no decision of the board can in any way be altered or appealed from. The contention of the board is that they interpret the act as it has been enacted by this parliament. Reference was made by the last speaker (Mr. Black, Yukon), and also, I think, by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) to the principle which ran through the whole
Supply-S.C.R.-Pensions

act of 1919. Nothing can be truer than their assertion in this regard. In 1919 a Pension Act was passed by this parliament providing for men who had served in the Canadian Expeditionary Force a pension for any disability incurred on service and also for any aggravation of a pre-existing disability, whether or not such disability was attributable to service. That was the condition that prevailed in 1920, when the act of 1919 was amended. It will be remembered that through an error peace was declared on the tenth of January, 1920; the real declaration of peace took place on the thirty-first of August, 1921. During the session of 1920 a special parliamentary committee dealt with pensions and reestablishment generally. It was thought during that session that peace had been declared; and if you read carefully the act of 1919 you will see that there is a special provision that after the declaration of peace pensions should be awarded in respect of death or disability when these were attributable to service. Now, in the session of 1920 an amendment was introduced to the Pension Act of 1919 repealing section 11, which was the vital section, and replacing it by the provision that pension should be awarded in respect of disability or death when such disability or death were the direct result of military service. I had at that time the advantage of being a member of the parliamentary committee, as I have been ever since the war with the exception of last year.

The minister was on that committee. Will he say it was the intention of the committee or of parliament at that time that that change should apply to members or ex-members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, or was it not the intention that the change should apply only to members of the permanent fprce?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I was coming to that: I could not speak of it before I had mentioned the fact that the law had been amended. Before the parliamentary committee representatives of the Pension board were heard and they stated definitely that the new section would not affect the Canadian Expeditionary Force men but would be applicable only to men who remained on service after the declaration of peace, having in mind undoubtedly the men of the permanent force. That act was passed by parliament and things went on until 1921, when another special parliamentary committee had to deal with pension matters. Then the words "as such" were added to the 1920 clause 11, and the clause in 1921 after that addition would

read about like this: Pensions shall be awarded when disabilities or death are attributable to military service as such. Again I think it was pointed out that that had reference only to men of the permanent force and that men of the Canadian Expeditionary Force would not be affected, that it did not change the practice with regard to them. Now the declaration of peace took place on the 31st day of August, 1921, and bearing in mind what the 1919 Pension Act said, that after the declaration of peace pensions would be awarded only in respect of disabilities or death attributable to war service, having also in mind the amendment of 1920 which did away with the insurance principle clause of 1919, and having also in mind this other amendment of 1921, the Pension board issued in the month of September, 1921, a minute in which it was stated that pensions henceforth would be awarded only when disabilities or death were attributable to military service. That altered to a large degree the practice that the Pension board had followed up to that time. I hope I make myself clear, but if I do not I would invite any question in order to make everybody absolutely satisfied that he understands the situation.
On what authority was that minute of the Pension board issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The Pension board does not require any authority at all to interpret the act. The act itself confides it to the discretion of the board to make their own interpretation, and moreover, my hon. friend being a lawyer and better versed in legal questions than I am knows as well as I do that if you read section 11 of the act as it was passed in 1920 it is plain that pensions can be awarded only when disabilities or death are attributable to military service. But as to what my hon. friend mentioned a moment ago, when this very limiting amendment was considered before the parliamentary committee it was then openly stated by the representatives of the board that this clause would apply only to men who remained on service after the declaration of peace and would not affect the members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. This minute was issued in the month of September, 1921, under the authority of the Pension board, and they have that authority; it is given to them.

Are they the final arbiters on the question of the interpretation of the law? Have they any method of referring, for instance to the Supreme Court?
