speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: They are the final arbiters. There is an appeal from the Pension board today, but it is an appeal from the Pension board to the Pension board, and that is the only appeal there is.
Do they not often get the opinion of the Justice department in interpreting the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
They do, but they are
not forced to do it. They may seek the opinion of the Department of Justice. In this instance they have sought the opinion of the Department of Justice on clause 11 as it now stands on the statute, and the Justice department, and I think properly so, replied that the board's interpretation of the letter of the act was correct. No one could say otherwise.
But what I have in mind, Mr. Chairman, are the declarations that were made before the parliamentary committee by the representatives of the Pension board to the effect that the new clause 11 would only apply to members of the permanent force, because as they said there is now no longer any Canadian Expeditionary Force. It was then made perfectly clear by the chairman of that committee, Mr. Cronyn, and by a number of hon. gentlemen who sat on that committee, and in particular by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs), that it would not affect the Canadian Expeditionary Force men. The clause as you read it in the act to-day does not refer at all to disabilities or death incurred on service, but only to disabilities or death which are the result of military service as such. Having said that much, I do not want to delay the committee much longer.
I may say that when the Pension board in 1921 issued that minute which placed upon their medical examiners the duty of awarding or recommending pension only to those who came within clause 11 of the new act of 1920, and 1921, the practice of the board and the practice of the medical examiners all over the country was naturally altered to a large degree. It was only a few months after that it was noticed that a stricter interpretation of what was thought to be the act was being applied by the Pension board and certain accusations were levelled against the Pension board. The rest of the story is known to every hon. member of this House. The accusations were investigated by a royal commission, which has taken a great deal of pains to get in contact with service men of every unit, and this royal commission has already submitted two reports bearing particularly upon pensions, appeals and insurance. The report has been placed in the hands of hon. members, and it is not for me to say what hon. members Bhould think of it.
As far as the charges against the Pension board of plot or conspiracy or ulterior motive are concerned, they have not been sustained. The royal commission has found, however, that the practice has been altered by the Pension board and that generally their policy had been unsympathetic, and that increased severity had taken place in the consideration of pension applications. If it could not be called undue severity, surely there was increased severity in dealing with applications for pensions. Now, the Ralston commission has submitted a number of recommendations in regard to the Pension Act. These recommendations I think will be carried out substantially by the bill which I shall introduce into the House, within two or three days, I hope. The resolution is already on the order paper which covers the main part of the bill.
May I ask, will the bill include reverting to the insurance principle so that the remainder of the expeditionary force can enjoy the same advantage as those who acted prior to September 1920?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Yes. I am not expected of course, to go into details at the present time. As minister in charge of the department I have been overwhelmed by complaints coming from ex-service men. I have a good deal of sympathy with most of my colleagues who have had two or three departments to administer during the last year. I think I might have as much sympathy for myself because I do not believe that the work performed by any other member of the government has been as arduous as the task that was mine during that time. I can fairly say that over 2,000 cases have been submitted to me for examination and for action. Those cases did not all have reference to pensions, but a large portion of them did. Others were treatment cases. Both classes in many instances, came together. Some hon. members, to-night or this afternoon, referred to their lack of success in submitting cases to the Pension board. Let me tell them that I have not been more fortunate than they have. Out of, I should say, about 1,000 cases, at least, of pensions submitted to the board for reconsideration I do not think that I have succeeded in more than 2 or 3 per cent. In other words the Pension board interpreted the act as they read it, and I do not believe that they will yield to any outside influence, which 1 think is something to their credit. I would not approve of their conduct if, in my cases though they might not be deserving, they should yield and award a pension. In many cases-I would not venture to state how many,
Supply-S.C.R.-Pensions

but in fifty cases at least-that I have submitted to the Pension board I believe that I would have given a different decision to the one they rendered. I may have been wrong but my impression was at that time [DOT]that pensions should have been awarded in those particular cases. However, the Pension board thought in their wisdom that the act would not permit them to award a pension.
You do not, Mr. Chairman, expect me to go into the individual cases that have been submitted this afternoon by different hon. members. Most of them, I think, have come to my knowledge. Some are very interesting, some are peculiar, some are very rare. In &, particular instance, I fancy, there is only *one case such as that referred to by one hon. member, and I scarcely think the Pension Act should be amended on that account. If the sentiment of the people of Canada, if the sentiment of the House of Commons and parliament generally, is that the act has not been properly interpreted by the Pension board, the only recourse is to amend the act and provide for an appeal. I do not know of any court in the British Empire, outside of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, that is without an appeal. In Great Britain there are thirty different district boards specially appointed for the purpose of dealing *with pensions and ex-soldiers. In the United States they had at first a very large number of district boards, but they have contracted this number gradually to fourteen. They now have fourteen district boards operating in the United States. There is an appeal from those district boards to another board in Washington, the exact evolution of which I forget. There is also an appeal from the decision of that second board, and finally an appeal from the third decision to the President of the United States.

Would the minister mind saying whether those appeals are in the nature of a rehearing of the case and of the evidence, or are the cases tried in the courts just as cases are tried here before a trial judge, the case going to appeal with the same evidence subject to addition where evidence is omitted by mistake?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Of course I do not think that is the proper method. I am, however, subject to conviction. Toronto, Ottawa, Hamilton and London have a combined population of at least one-third of the population of the whole province of Ontario. One-half of the appeals, I would judge, would come from those cities, and those appeals would have to come before those city tribunals. Is an ordinary court of justice a competent board? Can one imagine, for instance, all the files needed in the trials of some of these cases being removed from the units to the different county court divisions, in Ontario for example? The matter is quite different if the board sits in a city itself; it is within easy reach of the unit where the files of the men are available.
As to the constitution of the court; generally those courts will have only one judge. The boards must have men who are conversant with military matters, with veterans' claims generally, with veterans' ailments. Members of the board should know what conditions prevailed in the army, generally speaking, and that is why I presume the royal commission recommends that two of any three men should be ex-service men. I believe also the recommendation is made in this regard upon the insistence of returned men generally. I do not know that in England those cases are tried before the ordinary courts of law. I am informed, and I think credibly, that those boards have been appointed by the Minister of Pensions for the purpose of hearing cases and then appeals upon decisions.
I think I have dealt with almost every feature of this subject that has been brought up very moderately by hon. gentlemen. The question of dealing with veterans generally has never been in the past, from the moment I served on the parliamentary committee in 1919 to this day, a matter of
10	p.m. political cleavage. All the parliamentary committees from 1919 to last year have dealt with this question regardless of any political leanings that any member of it may have. This spirit has prevailed all through. I believe it is the intention of the people of Canada to give to the returned men a square deal,-justice-full justice-and if there is some remote measure of doubt in the case of a returned man, that he should get the benefit of the doubt, in other words, be treated with generosity. It will be in that spirit that I will submit, during the course of this week, I hope, the legislation that is intended.

What particular case had the minister in mind when he said some time ago that there was only one case of that type in existence, and, therefore, legislation dealing with that case would not be justified.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health

state in connection with the proposed legislation, whether he intended to deal with the construction of section 11 in its relation to section 25 (3), that being the section which states that "no deduction shall be made from the pension of any member of the forces who has served in a theatre of actual war" and who was admitted as being physically fit when he enlisted. It has been dealt with in

The minister pointed out
that the Pension board can act only within the statute. The minister made that statement fairly strongly himself. While he was speaking, I looked over half a dozen clauses, clauses 29, 31, 33, 34, 37, and in all those clauses I have given the numbers of, the term "in their discretion" or "in their opinion" is used. That is as to the granting of pensions, so that in many clauses of the Pension Act the board can act in their discretion or opinion. Therefore, they are not tied down to cast iron rules as the impression would be given by the minister or themselves. I wish to make that correction because I think it is only fair that that statement should be corrected. They are tied down to cast iron rules in many of the clauses; but in many others the matter is left to their discretion, and it is usually in those clauses that cases arise on which there are disputes.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Of course I am perfectly
aware that in the Pension Act a number of clauses give the Pension board wide discretionary powers. But I beg to differ from my hon. friend when he says that these discretionary clauses are the vital clauses of the act.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Well, I understood my hon. friend to say that most of the cases that were complained of came under those clauses.
I said that very many of the cases came under them, and I think they do.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not share my hon. friend's view, and I beg to differ humbly from his opinion. Most of the complaints are due to the interpretation or administration of two clauses of the act, clause 11, which is the vital section, providing for the award of pensions in the case of disability and death, and section 25, subsection 3, which deals with pre-existing disabilities in the case of men who served in any theatre of actual war. Outside of that, of course, there are a number of discretionary clauses. For instance, there are such clauses in the case of parents, grandparents, prospective dependency, dependent sisters, dependent brothers, any major child that has become of age but who for some reason or other may be incapacitated mentally or physically, and unable to earn his own living. If he were sound he would not receive a pension, supposing that he belonged to a pensioner, after the age of sixteen, and in the case of a girl after the age of seventeen. He might, however, be twenty-one and still be unable to earn his living, but in the discretion of the board he might be awarded a pension. In numberless cases of the kind discretionary powers are left with the board. No doubt there are some complaints in this regard, and my hon. friend is right in a measure. But if I have appreciated rightly the complaints that have come before me, most of them come within the category of disabilities on the part of men who claim a pension on that account, such disabilities having been incurred on service and not having been recognized by the board. There are a few cases of widows who claim a pension and are denied it because they married after the appearance of disability on the part of their husbands. Section 25, subsection 3, also caused a good deal of trouble in the matter of pre-existing disability in men who served in a theatre of actual war, undoubtedly the board have discretionary powers in many cases, and some of the complaints bear upon these matters.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Earlier in the session I brought to the attention of the minister one or two cases where pensions had been cancelled without notice to the persons receiving them. The person should be given every opportunity during a certain number of days, say ten days or two weeks, to explain any charge that may be made. I have no doubt there are many cases, apart from the ones that came to my personal notice, and I feel sure that the minister will agree that no pension should be suspended or discontinued without notice to the person entitled and an opportunity given of presenting his or her case to the board.

speechtext:
I am of the opinion that a notice is always served on the person concerned. I am very much surprised to hear

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend absolutely that in such cases they should be notified, say, a month ahead of the intention to discontinue their pensions in order that they might have sufficient time to make representations.

Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend The Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act by providing,-
(1) That in any case where an application for insurance under the said act has been received, and the applicant has died prior to the delivery to him of the policy of insurance, the approval of the application by the proper officer and the receipt of the initial premium shall be deemed to have been sufficient to put the insurance into force, unless it can be shown that the application was fraudulent, and any insurance
Returned Soldiers' Insurance

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
moneys which would have been payable had the policy been delivered to the applicant shall now be made payable, subject to a deduction of the amount of premium due from the date of application to the date of death.
(2) That any applications which were rejected prior to 1st July, 1922, under any conditions set forth in section 2 of the amending act of 1922, or the schedule thereto, shall be reviewed, except in cases where the applicant is suffering or has become impaired as a result of self-inflicted wounds or immoral conduct, or where the application was fraudulent, and provision be made to give the right on such review to any applicant now living to insure, and if the applicant has died, the amount of insurance for which he applied shall now be made payable, less the amount which would have be£n due as premium from the date of application to the date of death, notwithstanding that no effective insurance contract was completed, and provided that the application was approved.
He said: This resolution is for the purpose of carrying out the recommendation of the loyal commission respecting soldiers' insurance. Clause 1 applies to a few cases where the application for insurance had been filed with the department, had been approved and the premium paid, but the soldier died before the policy was delivered to him. It was held by the Finance department that in such cases no contract existed and the insurance money was not paid to the soldier's dependents. There are only six or seven such cases in all. This is to provide that when the application was regularly approved and the premium paid-

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Prior to death? The resolution does not state that.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is what it means.

speechtext:

Mr.	MANION:	All of them?Mr.	BELAND:	Yes.Mr.	POWER:	Would	the	minister explain what is meant in clause 1 by saying "unless it can be shown that the application was fraudulent?" Would he give us some examples of what	would	be	considered a

speechtext: No.

cases where the application had been passed on before death?

speechtext:
Clause 2 of the resolution
covers that. I stated when I gave notice of this resolution two or three days ago that there was a slight error made in the drafting of clause 2. The last line should not have read "provided that the application was approved' but "provided that such applicant lived for a sufficient period of time to admit of the approval of his application by the proper officer of the department in the ordinary course of procedure."
Perhaps a word of explanation is necessary in this connection. The intention when this Soldiers' Insurance Act was passed by parliament was that every returned soldier who made an application for insurance could insure, in other words, that every soldier should be insurable if he made application. I think in 1921, and especially in the month of January, 1922, some restrictions were made and enforced by the Pension board, which has the administration of this act together with the Minister of Finance, to the effect that the insurance money in the case of an application not being approved would not be payable, and also that certain applications on the part of men who were seriously ill of an illness which was not due to war service, and who moreover had no dependents, should not be entertained by the board or approved by the Minister of Finance. Hon. gentlemen will remember that during the session of 1922 we amended the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act to provide a certain schedule which sets out the conditions under which an application for insurance can be refused. That amendment was passed last year. The Returned Soldiers' Act was passed originally in 1920 and was made valid for the period of two years, so on the 1st September, 1922, it was coming to an end, but last year we extended the provisions of the act for one year making it applicable to the 1st September

S.C.R. Act Amendment
1923, with certain restrictions proposed in a schedule that was annexed to the act. But now we contend, and I think it is only fair, that all the men, no matter what physical condition they may have been in who filed their applications before the 1st July, 1922, that is the time the act was amended with the schedule, should be insurable and in case of death their dependents will receive the insurance money. I asked the department to supply me with a report in this connection and they gave me the following figures which, perhaps, are not absolutely needed in this instance but which may be of interest to hon. members:	Total number of policies issued as of March 31st, 1923, 19,516, with a value of 846,864,500. Total number of death claims as of March 31st, 1923, 514. I may say en passant that this is not a very large rate. The value of these claims is $1,622,500. The total number of claims settled under section 10, insurance cancelled by award of pension, was 109.

It is represented that these men had, under the original act, the privilege of insuring their lives only by making application, without any medical examination and regardless of their physical condition. Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Act, and to provide:-
1.	That the power to make regulations for the constitution of medical boards, including appeal boards, with such powers as may be deemed expedient, be repealed, and provision be made to give the minister power, with the approval of the Governor in Council, to make regulations for appeals from decisions as to the right of ex-members of the forces to treatment with pay and allowances, and for that purpose to designate the review and appeal tribunals to be constituted under the proposed amendments to the Pension Act.
2.	That the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the minister, appoint an ex-member of the forces to be an Official Soldiers' Adviser in each unit or district of the department, at such salary or remuneration as may be decided in each case, with prescribed duties.
3.	That the minister shall have power to appoint a person or persons to hear and receive evidence on oath in respect of any matter pertaining to the department or procedure of the department.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Under the Pension Act
resolution which is now on the order paper it will be seen that a certain number of appeal boards will be constituted in different units throughout the country. The Pension Act, however, only deals with pensions. It is desired also to provide appeals for those ex-members of the force who are seeking treatment with pay and allowances. As hon. members are aware a number of men apply for treatment and are denied treatment with pay and allowance by the Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment board. As the right has been granted to appeal from a decision of the Pension board it is also proposed that the right shall be granted, in cases where treatment is denied, to appeal from the decision of headquarters to the boards that will be constituted under the Pension Act.
374G

S.C.R. Act Amendment
The second portion of the resolution provides for the appointment of a soldier adviser in every unit of the department, thus following the example which has been set in England. In every one of the thirty units in that country there is a soldier adviser who is paid by the government to give advice to the men who desire to appeal, that is, to examine their claim, and to advise them as to the propriety of appealing or not appealing, and to present their case before the board. In other words to represent' them. This has been asked by the men generally throughout Canada and it has been recommended by the royal commission.
The third part of the resolution is a provision to give power to these investigators of the department to receive evidence on oath. This provision exists for the Pension board. In the Pension Act there is a clause, I do not remember which one, which provides that the investigators or the examiners of the Pension board can receive evidence on oath. We have numberless investigations to make in connection with treatment and with pensions. The officials of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment have no power to swear a person who gives evidence in these cases, and this provision is designed to prevent fraud as much as possible.

speechtext: There will be twenty-seven appointments to be made in pursuance of this provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: At what proposed salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That will come under the Pension Act Bill. If my hon. friend desires to discuss it now, I can give him the information.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I just asked as to the proposed salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The salary for the men who will serve on the appeal boards is not fixed. I did not intend to make that position a permanent one. I had in view-and I think it is also the recommendation of the royal commission-that these men should serve part time, and that they should be paid so much per day when they are called upon to sit on a certain number of appeals that are brought in by the unit. When a number of appeals has accumulated, the members of that board should be called together and will discharge their duties during one, two or three days in a month, or more, as the number of appeals would warrant, and they will be paid so much per day. We thought that-it would be a good deal more economical than to pay a regular salary and have these men devote the whole of their time to the work. It is presumed that during the first six months, or perhaps during the first year, the number of appeals will be very large, but after one year the number will decrease considerably. Then it is provided in the bill that we can contract the appeal board to the number which will be required; in other words, to extend the territorial limits of these appeal boards. Some of the men who were heard by the royal commission submitted the view that there should be one in every unit and were very insistent upon it. Others expressed the view that, perhaps, if we had three or four all over Canada it would be sufficient. But the commission has recommended specifically that in each unit there should be an appeal board and I think my hon. friend from the Yukon (Mr. Black), if I mistake not, referred to the great patronage that would develop therefrom. I can assure my hon. friend that I do not see it in the same light. My idea is not to exercise any patronage in this regard. The aim will be to secure three outstanding men in each one of those cities where the unit is located, who would commend themselves to public confidence and to the confidence of the returned men generally, regardless of their political leanings. I may say that the royal commission itself contained one Liberal, one Independent, and one Conservative.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Who was the Conservative?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Dr. McKeown.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Has my hon. friend any doubt about it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, I have.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Entirely wrong.

S.C.R. Act Amendment

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Liberal-Conservative.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is an ameliorated Conservative.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am afraid there is simply amelioration and no conservatism.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If my hon friend knew of the protests I have received from my Liberal friends because I did not make the appointments strictly Liberal, he would agree with me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Has the minister considered the matter of having the appointmen! of the official soldier advisers made by the Civil Service Commission? It seems to me, at least, that there should be some good reason for having them appointed otherwise than by the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest they should be appointed by that commission?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have not the remotest objection.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Have they power to appoint temporary officials?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Give them power to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No objection whatever. I would be pleased.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it the intention to proceed with the bills to-morrow? If so, we would require to get copies early in the morning because we want to look at them.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, it is not the intention, because they would not be distributed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend will see that these bills are distributed early, because we would like to see them some time in advance of their being taken up in the House.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: As to the procedure before the appeal boards, will the boards merely review the evidence that appears on the files, or will [DOT] they themselves hear evidence?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is provided that the man himself has the right to appear personally before that board.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Before the appeal board?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, and he may submit whatever evidence he likes which is not already on the file, and the soldier adviser in this connection will be most useful to us. In that connection I would point out that I undertake before this House to appoint the soldier adviser that will be indicated to me by the returned soldiers' associations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is recommended by the commission, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think it is. The Civil Service Commission will suit me absolutely, if it suits the House. This is an appointment made by the soldiers themselves-their own representative.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is the soldier adviser to be paid fees or salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I presume these men will receive a retainer of so much a month. I presume the adviser will be a lawyer. That, of course, is in the hands of the soldiers themselves. If they should appoint a lawyer, we should provide, *in accordance with the number of pensioners in the unit, what should be a fair monthly remuneration for him for whatever time he gives to the work of advising the soldiers generally.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: There is a reference to the official soldier adviser in each unit or district ; what is the distinction between unit and district?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: There is a distinction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: So that the intention of the minister is to appoint a soldier adviser in each unit? If I remember rightly Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia are all one unit?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: So that the man from Prince Edward Island, in order to have his case properly prepared, would have to consult his official adviser in Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Would it not be well to have an official adviser in Charlottetown or St. John, if it comes under the same unit? I would make that suggestion to the minister, owing to the difficulty of the men communieat-ing with the adviser under the other arrangement. I think the minister should look into that. We have the same situation in Quebec. We happen to be under the control of the headquarters in Montreal. It is extremely difficult and inconvenient for pensioners in Quebec to have to consult the adviser or somebody in Montreal in regard to their pensions.
I would suggest to the minister that, in cases where applicants are far removed from the headquarters an adviser should be appointed in some more convenient place. This seems to be a good job; let us give everybody a chance.	'

Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend The Pension Act, chapter 43 of the statutes of 1919, and the amending acts, and to provide,-
1.	That enactments be made respecting pensions for military services rendered during the war and after the war, which shall be made retroactive to the first day of September, 1919, and all cases in which pension has been refused, reduced, discontinued or underrated by reason of the fact that the proposed legislation was not included in the Pension Act shall be subject to review by the Board of Pension Commissioners, and on such review pension shall be granted, increased or continued as from the date or dates it would have been granted, increased or continued had such proposed legislation been in force when such refusal, reduction or discontinuance or underrating was made effective.
2.	That the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice may appoint a District Review Board for each of the nine districts of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and a Federal Appeal Board for Canada, to review appeals from decisions of the Board of Pension Commissioners ; and that provision be made for the tenure of office and qualifications of the members of such boards, and for the payment of their remuneration or salaries out of any unappropriated moneys of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
3.	That the Governor in Council may make such rules and regulations as are deemed necessary to carry out and enforce the provisions of the proposed legislation.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

Is it proposed to
make the decisions before these district review boards, if favourable to the applicant, final, or are they only intermediary? Must applications go to the Pension board, be refused, then go to the district review board and then, in any event, go to the federal appeal board again? Will these boards not have power to deal finally if dealing favourably to the applicant?

Canada Shipping Act

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
All appeals, after theyl
have been dealt with by the district appeal! board, must come back to the Board of Pen-j sion Commissioners. In the case of a more| favourable decision rendered by the district-appeal board, the pension board will carry it out; but should they refuse to carry it out, it will automatically go to the federal appeal board for confirmation. Then the Board of Pension Commissioners shall be bound by the decision of the appeal board. In the case that the Board of Pension Commissioners carries out the decision of the district appeal board, the decision is final. In every case where the decision of the district appeal board is not more favourable to the applicant than the decision appealed against, it will automatically, through the Board of Pension Commissioners, go to the federal appeal board.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Beland thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 205, to amend the Pension Act.
